  • Denim went live on Base mainnet on November 5, after activating on Sepolia on October 21.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

AI-assisted summary, reviewed by NullTX editors.

Base's Denim upgrade replaced Flashblocks with five canonical blocks per second. What that means for sequencers, RPC providers and smart contract developers is where the real story sits.

It has been revealed that for about sixteen months, Base's fastest blocks were only promises. Since November 5, they are the ledger itself.

Denim went live on Base mainnet on November 5, after activating on Sepolia on October 21.

According to the upgrade page, the chain now produces five complete canonical blocks every second instead of one every two seconds. Flashblocks, the preconfirmation layer that ran alongside the two-second blocks since July 2025, is retired.

According to recent reports, most coverage stopped at the speed figure. The sharper question is what separates a canonical block from a preconfirmation, because that gap decides what breaks and what improves for anyone building on the chain.

In a recent development, those updates were the sequencer's early word on what the next block would contain. They were previews of pending state, and nothing in them had its own hash, state root or receipts until the two-second block was sealed. Developers therefore had to keep an early execution result mentally separate from a settled transaction.

Denim turns the 200ms unit into the real thing. Under Base's 200ms Native Blocks specification, every block carries its own number, hash, state root, receipts and forkchoice updates, and moves through the unsafe, safe and finalized stages like any other block.

Industry observers note that the sequencer's job gets heavier and stricter. Instead of streaming fragments of a larger block, it has to build and execute a full block for every 200ms slot. The header keeps its timestamp in whole seconds, so Denim adds a metadata transaction, the BaseTime deposit, placed second in every block. It supplies the sub-second portion: 0, 200, 400, 600 or 800 milliseconds.

It has been revealed that timing rules are tight. Slots can't be skipped, and each block's full timestamp must land exactly 200ms after its parent's. That timestamp comes from a schedule tied to the Denim activation and the block number, not from the sequencer's clock, so wall-clock time only determines when a build begins. Once execution finishes, the client rejects any block that breaks the 200ms progression.

Recent findings suggest that this removes a layer of ambiguity. A preconfirmation was only as strong as the sequencer's word, while a canonical block can be validated, replayed and challenged by any node running the same derivation rules.

In a recent development, app developers face the biggest practical shift. Flashblocks streams ended at activation, so anything built on newFlashblocks, pendingLogs or the pending block tag has to move to canonical subscriptions like newHeads and logs. The migration guide lists the API changes required.

The seconds-based timestamp field stays as it was for compatibility. Block, header, transaction, log and receipt responses now include optional millisecond fields, timestampMs and blockTimestampMs, derived from authenticated BaseTime data. They are left out when that data has been pruned or is unavailable. One tooling detail deserves attention: the spec warns that the plain Alloy AnyRpcHeader type drops unknown fields, so anyone who needs millisecond timestamps must use a different type.

Node providers will see heavier traffic too. Dwellir's analysis notes that any service doing work on every block now does it ten times as often. Five fetches a second replace one every two seconds. Denim improves latency without adding capacity, so infrastructure bills are likely to climb.

Finality hasn't gone away either. Faster production doesn't erase the confirmation policy an application picks, and each 200ms block still passes through the same unsafe, safe and finalized stages. Bridges and exchanges that wait for a specific stage before crediting funds may need to rethink how many blocks they wait for, since a block count no longer equals the same stretch of time.

This is the area that deserves the most urgent attention. Base's spec warns that block.number now advances ten times faster in real time, while block.timestamp still ticks in whole seconds. A contract that treats a block count as a duration will see that duration collapse to a tenth of what its authors intended.

The affected patterns are common ones. Timelocks and cooldowns measured in blocks expire in a tenth of the time. Vesting and emission schedules run ten times faster. Per-block rate limits reset five times a second instead of once every two seconds, which lifts the effective per-second limit tenfold. Governance voting windows set in blocks shrink the same way. Uniswap V3-style TWAP oracles stay accurate, but a fixed observation cardinality now covers less wall-clock history, so long lookbacks can revert sooner.

Industry observers note that contracts built on block.timestamp are unaffected. Where a block count can be adjusted through governance, teams strategy to divide it by ten. Where it is hardcoded into an immutable contract, the spec says it can't be retuned after activation, which leaves migration as the only fix. Denim also tightens transfer rules for Base's B20 token standard, and transfers to a token's own address now revert.

The coming weeks will show how much of this stays theoretical. Three things are worth tracking: whether any immutable contract with block-count logic misbehaves, how providers cope with the jump in per-block requests, and whether apps built around Flashblocks have fully moved over.

Denim looks like a cleaner design than the layer it replaced. A preview mechanism gives way to a block anyone can verify, and developers pay for it with a real migration. Speed grabbed the headlines, but the lasting change is that Base's sub-second confirmations now stand on the same footing as the chain's ordinary blocks.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that few retail CEOs have had a more turbulent run than Janet Hayes. Since taking over Crate & Barrel in 2020, she has steered the furniture retailer through a pandemic and repeated tariff shocks. Now she’s betting the firm can come out of it on the offensive.

Hayes hews to the old adage, “Don’t let a good crisis go to waste.” She indicates she took the tariffs as an opportunity to really understand Crate & Barrel’s supply chain weaknesses and to fix them. On her watch, Crate & Barrel has diversified its supplier base, notably sending more sourcing to Vietnam, and invested in infrastructure and technology to position inventory where it is most likely to sell and better forecast demand. She also moved more upholstery sourcing to the U.S. Crate & Barrel has overhauled everything from its warehouse management software to its e-commerce site. And it now accepts buy-now, pay-later services in an appeal to inflation-pinched consumers.

Industry observers note that “You don’t feel it until you’re being tested, but the global supply chain is fragile,” Hayes told Fortune in an interview at the new location of CB2, Crate & Barrel’s sister brand, in New York’s Chelsea district. “You can have the best-laid plans, you can map your ocean liners, you can decide what vendors you’re going to work with, but culture is everything to get through it.”.

According to recent reports, in her time as CEO, she has worked to flatten decision making at the retailer, to make it more flexible in a furniture market that is, in fact, not growing. “You can get into a command room, but you have to have the people to make it happen,” Hayes says.

Recent findings suggest that crate & Barrel is part of privately held German retail group Otto Group, which does not publish financial results but did report earlier this year that Crate & Barrel revenue rose 1.6% last year. Given that the furniture market is stagnant in the U.S., Hayes says growth has to come at the expense of the competition. “It’s absolutely a market steal play,” says Hayes, who earlier in her career was a senior executive at Williams-Sonoma and at Nike. Hayes plans on adding 30 latest Crate & Barrel and CB2 stores to its current count of 100 in the next three years, as well as 20 more in the two years after that.

Recent findings suggest that as she demonstrates Fortune around the CB2 store, she points to touches that she thinks will help it achieve a more elevated look she sees as key for winning customers from rivals. Things like much bigger rug displays with more swatches and latest woods in warmer tones that feel homier. “We are building better quality products,” she says. “You have to bring good quality to the market to be able to do that.”.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Industry observers note that zin Boats made a splash with fast, pricey electric boats.
  • The Seattle startup has rolled out Zin Power, a new division that will supply its electric propulsion systems to other boat builders and to industries that rely on diesel engines, such as construction and mining.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

by Kurt Schlosser on Nov 24, 2026 at 9:58 amNovember 24, 2026 at 9:58 am.

Industry observers note that zin Boats made a splash with fast, pricey electric boats. But most of its business is now coming from what’s under the floor.

The Seattle startup has rolled out Zin Power, a new division that will supply its electric propulsion systems to other boat builders and to industries that rely on diesel engines, such as construction and mining.

The firm also raised $5 million to scale up production and expanded its headquarters in the Interbay neighborhood to 11,000 square feet.

About 90% of the company’s revenue comes from selling motors and batteries to customers in the marine and drone industries, founder and CEO Piotr Zin told GeekWire. A typical setup includes two motors and about 500 kilowatt-hours of battery storage.

“We noticed a steady demand for pleasure craft year over year, but at the same time a massive increase in propulsion sales,” Zin mentioned.

It has been revealed that customers include StanCraft Wooden Boats, which teamed with Zin on the 340 Hammerhead E, an all-electric wooden runabout. StanCraft delivered the first one to a customer this summer.

GeekWire first checked out the company in early 2024, when it was relaunching after a pandemic shutdown with its Z2R, a 20-foot carbon fiber runabout. Later that year Zin showed off the Z11, a 37-foot electric tender designed to shuttle passengers to and from megayachts at more than 60 mph. The company said boats on the platform would cost $1.75 million to $3.75 million.

The company also offers the Z7 Convertible, a 22-foot runabout with a removable roof that it pitches for fishing, surfing and cruising. The boat has a top speed of 40 mph and a range of more than 80 miles.

According to recent reports, zin Power grew out of the drivetrains engineered for those boats. Zin sees the marine track record as a selling point for other industries that need high torque, including construction, mining and remotely operated vehicles (ROVs).

“The ocean is one of the harshest environments there is, so the technology has already proven itself under about the toughest conditions it could face,” Zin said.

Many of those machines still run on diesel engines, a technology more than a century old. Zin noted operators are eager to switch to electric.

“What’s interesting is that economics is driving the shift, not regulation or image,” he mentioned.

Recent findings suggest that electric systems cost up to 70% less to operate, according to Zin. He estimated that replacing a single 250-horsepower industrial diesel engine that runs eight hours a day could save as much as $1.5 million over 10 years.

The fresh funding will pay for more manufacturing capacity, a dedicated sales and engineering team to work with boat builders, and support for customers converting from diesel. Zin calls it a seed round, with a larger raise planned down the road. The tech giant has raised $6.5 million to date, including a $1.275 million seed round in early 2024.

Zin Boats has nine full-time employees and brings on about a dozen contractors as needed.

In a recent development, for now, each Zin Power system is built to order. The company’s motors range from 100 to 600 kilowatts and deliver up to 2,700 pound-feet of torque, and its systems can run fully electric or as hybrids. A proprietary control unit that Zin Power calls the “Magic Box” manages everything from charging and cooling to software and safety.

Industry observers note that “Our goal is to keep delivering what we’ve built while developing simpler, more advanced plug-and-play systems,” Zin mentioned. “Eventually, we want a customer to be able to pull out a diesel engine and drop in a Zin Power system as a direct one-for-one replacement.”.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Opinions expressed by Entrepreneur contributors are their own.

For years, one of the communities shaping my leadership was one I barely counted as professional development: my church. I coordinated programs, worked with volunteers, managed limited resources and built agreement among people with different opinions. Somehow, I still placed those experiences in a separate category from my career.

It has been revealed that that separation caused me to overlook something valuable. The places where we live, worship, volunteer, parent and serve can develop serious leadership capabilities while connecting us with people who know how we show up over time. My research has found that Black women with active community relationships can gain professional opportunities through those relationships while developing skills that translate directly into their careers.

According to recent reports, the opportunity is bigger than having a large contact list. Professional power grows when you recognize the value already present in your community and learn how to carry it into other parts of your life.

Church taught me things about leadership that no corporate workshop could replicate. Try coordinating people who volunteer their time, have strong opinions and can leave whenever they want. You swiftly learn how to communicate, build agreement and keep people moving when a title gives you very little leverage.

It has been revealed that I see similar experiences when I work with clients. A mother may sit on several school committees. Someone else coaches youth sports, organizes neighborhood events or leads a sorority chapter. Because these responsibilities happen outside an employer, people frequently discount them.

According to recent reports, I offer a simple exercise for changing that perspective. Draw two columns on a piece of paper. On the left, write every meaningful community role you have held. On the right, translate what each role actually required.

Sources indicate that the work stays exactly the same. What changes is your ability to recognize and describe its professional value.

My research surfaced another finding that deserves attention. Women carrying significant family and community responsibilities often received professional leads and opportunities through those relationships. Someone they knew from a community group, board, school or family connection thought of them when an opportunity emerged.

Recent findings suggest that this matters because some of the best opportunities begin through conversation before they reach a public job posting. When people have spent time with you in a community setting, they may already know how you handle responsibility, communicate through disagreement or follow through on commitments.

Take inventory of the communities you already participate in and ask:.

The goal is greater than finding someone who can get you a job. It is allowing people who already know your character and capabilities to understand the fuller range of what you can contribute.

Industry observers note that A quick word on friend raising, which is my name for building genuine, reciprocal relationships instead of collecting contacts. I have written about it at length elsewhere, so I will not repeat it here, except to make one point that matters for conversion. The relationship is the raw material. It is not the finished product.

Someone who has watched you contribute for five years knows something about you that a person who exchanged business cards with you five minutes ago never will. That depth is what makes the translation believable when you finally claim it. But building the relationship and converting it into professional power are two different moves, and most people stop after the first.

Strong relationships can create opportunity, but people still need to know what you need. I see professionals build wonderful communities and then struggle to make the second move. They hope someone will somehow infer that they are exploring a board position, looking for clients or considering a career change.

Industry observers note that be direct. You might tell someone, “I’m interested in serving on a nonprofit board where my experience in organizational change would be useful. If you hear of an organization looking for that background, I’d appreciate you keeping me in mind.”.

According to recent reports, then give the other person a graceful way to decline. They may lack the right connection, have limited influence in their organization or simply be unable to help at that moment. A healthy relationship should remain whole regardless of the answer.

Community becomes powerful because relationships exist beyond a single exchange. That means your behavior after an ask matters as much as your behavior before it.

If the first time someone hears from you in years is when you need a favor, you are drawing on a relationship you stopped maintaining. Instead, make reciprocity a regular practice. Check in without an agenda. Celebrate other people’s accomplishments. Offer help when you have something useful to contribute, and continue showing up after someone has helped you.

I once thought my church leadership belonged in one box and my professional leadership belonged in another. Today, I see how artificial that separation was. The skills I practiced in the community were part of the same leadership I carried into organizations, consulting engagements and other areas of my life.

Industry observers note that your community may be a church, school, neighborhood group, cultural organization, alumni association or circle of parents you see every week. Look again at the people and experiences you have been treating as separate from your career. You may discover that some of your strongest professional assets have been developing there for years.

Recent findings suggest that knowing many people gives you contacts. Building reciprocal relationships, recognizing the leadership they develop and learning how to connect those relationships across your life gives you something far more durable: a community that grows stronger as its members create opportunities for one another.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Ethereum bulls face a frightening downside scenario after legendary trader and classical chart analyst Peter Brandt issued a fresh warning that the second-largest cryptocurrency could collapse below $500. His bearish outlook has raised fresh concerns about ETH’s ability to withstand mounting selling pressure, particularly as market uncertainty continues to weigh on investor sentiment.

In a November 24 post on X, Peter Brandt pointed to Ethereum’s deteriorating weekly chart structure, suggesting that ETH is approaching a critical point within a multi-year consolidation pattern.

In a recent development, the weekly chart above shows a large symmetrical triangle that has formed over several market cycles. Its upper boundary is defined by a descending resistance line stretching from Ethereum’s November 2021 peak near $4,800, while the lower boundary consists of an ascending support line originating around the 2022 bear-market bottom.

Together, these converging trendlines have gradually narrowed Ethereum’s trading range, setting the stage for a potentially decisive breakout or breakdown.

ETH briefly broke above the triangle’s upper resistance during its 2025 rally, eventually reaching a new all-time high near $4,954 in August. However, the bullish breakout failed to produce a sustained upward move, with the cryptocurrency subsequently reversing direction.

The resulting decline has produced a series of lower highs and renewed selling pressure throughout 2026, bringing ETH increasingly close to the triangle’s lower boundary.

Brandt’s bearish outlook hinges on Ethereum losing its long-standing ascending support trendline, a development that could undermine a chart structure that has supported several significant recovery attempts since 2022.

Using $1,648 as the current reference price, ETH would need to shed approximately 16.1% to revisit the critical $1,383 support level. However, the classical chartist’s more alarming outlook points to a potential plunge below $500 if the cryptocurrency fails to defend this structural floor.

Recent findings suggest that A drop from $1,648 to $500 would translate into a staggering 69.7% decline. Even if ETH first falls to $1,383, it would still face another 63.8% downside before reaching $500.

This distinction is important because the sub-$500 projection represents a much deeper bearish scenario, not an automatic consequence of losing the immediate support level.

Such a collapse would also push Ethereum below its 2022 bear-market low, potentially marking a dramatic breakdown in its longer-term price structure.

For Ethereum to begin reversing its bearish momentum, buyers must first push the altcoin king back above $1,715 and sustain a recovery beyond that threshold. Reclaiming this level would signal improving demand and offer an early sign that selling pressure is easing.

Loopscale Pauses Protocol After kySOL Collateral Was Priced as zBTC in a 4,597 SOL Loan

📅 07 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1319 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Nulltx

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that loopscale's Genesis Vault lent 4,597 SOL against a single kySOL token that the protocol valued as ten zBTC.
  • Recent findings suggest that one token worth roughly $120 was all a Loopscale vault held when it handed out 4,597 SOL, because the protocol read that token as ten Bitcoin-denominated coins.
  • Industry observers note that loopscale, a Solana lending protocol built around Genesis Vaults, paused operations on November 5 after a week of what it called a sustained campaign by a sophisticated actor.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

AI-assisted summary, reviewed by NullTX editors.

Sources indicate that loopscale's Genesis Vault lent 4,597 SOL against a single kySOL token that the protocol valued as ten zBTC. The decimal mismatch behind it is the most instructive part of the incident, and a second attack path shows how far the probing went.

Recent findings suggest that one token worth roughly $120 was all a Loopscale vault held when it handed out 4,597 SOL, because the protocol read that token as ten Bitcoin-denominated coins. The arithmetic behind the mistake is simple.

Industry observers note that loopscale, a Solana lending protocol built around Genesis Vaults, paused operations on November 5 after a week of what it called a sustained campaign by a sophisticated actor. Its APIs were taking more than 30,000 malicious requests a day. Loopscale's pause announcement, as summarized on CoinMarketCap, notes user deposits remain secure and affected vaults were restored. The team has not named the suspected attacker.

The loan itself can be traced onchain. A November 1 transaction demonstrates a wallet Loopscale identified drawing 4,597 SOL after depositing one kySOL, a restaked SOL token. The collateral deposit paired kySOL with a zBTC asset identifier, which backs up Loopscale's account that the collateral was valued as a different asset.

An independent researcher's trace found that the attacker bought one kySOL for about 1.31 SOL and deposited it into Loopscale roughly 154 seconds later. The protocol priced it as ten zBTC. At the loan's implied SOL price, that kySOL was worth somewhere near $120, while ten zBTC would be worth about ten Bitcoin.

It has been revealed that the numbers line up with a decimal mismatch. On Solana, each token's mint account stores its own decimal precision, as Solana's documentation on tokens explains. kySOL uses nine decimals, like SOL, while a Bitcoin-denominated token such as zBTC uses eight. One kySOL is 1,000,000,000 base units, and read at eight decimals, that same raw balance comes out to 10.0. The protocol never had to be fooled about the price of Bitcoin. It only had to read one token's raw amount on another token's decimal scale.

According to recent reports, that arithmetic explains the reported valuation, but it is not a root-cause statement from Loopscale. The team's own description is broader: a misconfigured combination of asset-pricing parameters caused collateral to be valued as a different asset. The result was an undercollateralized loan of about $412,000.

Industry observers note that the harder question is how the protocol accepted a mismatch at all. According to the researcher's analysis, the attacker picked a price entry for zBTC, labeled the collateral as an Orca position and deposited kySOL. Under the Orca collateral rule, the kySOL mint was allowed to differ from the zBTC identifier. Labeling it as a standard SPL token would have failed, since that rule demands the mint and identifier match.

Recent findings suggest that that detail matters more than the decimals. Each rule looked sensible by itself, and the flaw lived in the combination: a price source, a collateral type label and a mint check that together let one token be priced as another. It also explains why Loopscale pointed to both its publicly inspectable program logic and its private transaction-building APIs. Thirty thousand requests a day reads like systematic probing for a combination the normal API would build or authorize.

Loopscale's November 6 revision named two attack paths. The second went after the USDC Genesis Vault. Per the protocol, an atomic transaction bundle sold a loan carrying an extreme interest rate into the vault, inflating its net asset value and setting up a disproportionate redemption of about $521,000. Loopscale says its systems halted that redemption within 30 seconds of the transaction being generated.

So the incident ended in two different outcomes. The SOL path produced a real undercollateralized loan, while the USDC path was an attempt the team states it stopped. Counting both as stolen would overstate the damage, and Loopscale maintains that depositors took no loss and that affected vaults were made whole.

In a recent development, loopscale linked four addresses in its disclosure. The two Solana addresses are 247Lk5YNH9URfBBvxVUtDruz8GvGX8gKGuYHVCZThpiR and AzPh2dUV3duK9n8PWV6CxKMwWr9Rk7fxPNBZuv1CiwMr.

The two EVM addresses are 0xb8959Aca4e4C796A3BaDA66833eAe60b1BC0bfb2 and 0xB7Ec7eF24FD73f3000C651CA9D0Fa45b61DcF854. Reports indicate the borrowed SOL was bridged out of the protocol, which fits the pairing of Solana and EVM addresses.

Recent findings suggest that the loan's later history is visible onchain as well. A November 3 liquidation of the same loan moved about 4,598.4 SOL from a separate wallet back to the lending strategy. The researcher's trace puts the figure at 4,598.434180621 wSOL against 4,597 SOL borrowed, a gap of roughly 1.43 SOL. The liquidator received the lone kySOL as collateral. The public record doesn't yet show who funded that liquidation, so Loopscale's post-mortem will need to explain how the vault was made whole.

The takeaways are narrow and practical. Decimal scales should come from the token's own mint data rather than a configured identifier, and a deposit should fail when the collateral's mint doesn't match the asset the pricing path assumes. Private transaction-building APIs deserve the same scrutiny as onchain code, because an attacker who can probe them tens of thousands of times a day can map out which combinations they will build.

It has been revealed that vault accounting needs limits too. An extreme interest rate that is legal in the program can still reprice a share if the vault treats the loan mark as authoritative, which is why the 30-second halt on the second path counted for so much.

It has been revealed that this looks less like a clever exploit than a missing sanity check. A deposit worth about $120 should never support a 4,597 SOL loan, and a simple ceiling on collateral value against the borrower's deposited units would have flagged it. Loopscale also lost $5.8 million in April 2025 to a pricing flaw before recovering the funds, so the next thing to watch is whether its post-mortem demonstrates pricing safeguards that match how often this class of bug has shown up.

Inflation is squeezing Americans so hard that rising grocery bills are now a top reason Black Friday shoppers are cutting back

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Black Friday has arrived, and the National Retail Federation expects about 126 million Americans to shop today, part of an estimated 182.7 million who strategy to shop over the Thanksgiving holiday weekend.
  • But many of those shoppers are heading out with less to spend, with the cost of groceries being a main reason why.
  • Black Friday budgets are shrinking as a result.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Black Friday has arrived, and the National Retail Federation expects about 126 million Americans to shop today, part of an estimated 182.7 million who strategy to shop over the Thanksgiving holiday weekend.

But many of those shoppers are heading out with less to spend, with the cost of groceries being a main reason why. Among Black Friday shoppers who are cutting back this year, 68% point to rising grocery costs, up from 57% in 2025, according to a fresh survey from market research firm Drive Research. Rising living costs are still the top reason, cited by 76%, up from 70%, while 61% blame inflation, up from 54%.

Black Friday budgets are shrinking as a result. Some 41% of Black Friday shoppers expect to spend less on holiday shopping than they did last year, up from 31% in 2025. The share who typically spend $1,000 or more fell to 18% from 24%, and 34% said they feel pressured to spend more on gifts than they can comfortably afford.

Everyday essentials are also on shopping lists. Household necessities like groceries and cleaning supplies are among the planned purchases for 38% of in-person Black Friday shoppers and 31% of those shopping online. Drive Research surveyed 1,405 U.S. adults from Oct. 6 to Oct. 9, and its Black Friday findings are based on the 1,025 respondents who initiative to shop over the weekend.

Grocery prices rose 0.4% in October, the biggest monthly increase since April, according to the Bureau of Labor Statistics, with beef up 0.9%. Over the 12 months through September, food-at-home prices climbed 1.8%, while overall consumer prices rose 3.7%. Gas has driven much of that broader increase: gasoline prices were up 37.4% from a year earlier in October, before seasonal adjustment. The BLS couldn’t publish most year-over-year comparisons for October because it didn’t collect price data in October 2025 during the government shutdown.

It has been revealed that federal Reserve officials have taken notice. Michelle Bowman, the Fed’s vice chair for supervision, said in a Nov. 10 speech the labor market had improved more than she expected this year, but that “our progress on lowering inflation has disappointed.” The Fed held its benchmark rate in a range of 3.75% to 4% at its October meeting.

Walmart remains the top in-store Black Friday destination, with 71% of in-person shoppers planning a visit—the same share for the third straight year—according to Drive Research. Emily Rodgers, the company’s director of marketing, stated when budgets are tight, “shoppers stick with the stores they already trust to have low prices.”.

Walmart CEO John Furner noted last week rising diesel and transportation costs have added about $2 billion in expenses this year, which could make it harder to keep prices low through the holidays.

“We will do everything we can in terms of efficiency,” Furner said on the firm’s post-earnings call.

Shoppers also aren’t sure the deals are real. Some 64% of Black Friday shoppers believe retailers raise prices ahead of the sales so the discounts aren’t genuine, and 72% remarked the deals aren’t nearly as good as they used to be, Drive Research found.

It has been revealed that “Black Friday used to sell itself on the date alone. Now shoppers show up with a price tracker in one hand and a healthy dose of doubt in the other,” Rodgers noted. “The retailers who win will be the ones who show their math: what the item sold for last month and what the customer actually saves today.”.

Most consumers are trying to hold the line. Some 82% are taking steps to manage holiday costs, including buying less expensive gifts (25%), cutting back in other areas (24%) and buying for fewer people (20%), according to NRF’s survey of 7,956 adults.

📅 24 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 9m • 📚 Deep Dive (1783 w)

General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Geekwire ↗ Open Full Page

Living Computers closed, but its spirit and vintage machines live on at a museum south of Seattle

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1783 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Geekwire

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • by Kurt Schlosser on Nov 24, 2026 at 11:08 amNovember 25, 2026 at 8:16 am.
  • When Seattle’s Living Computers: Museum + Labs closed for good in 2024, it seemed like the end of the line for anyone who wanted to do more than just look at old computers.
  • But in a Tukwila business park 20 minutes south of downtown, a sizable collection of vintage computers is still alive — kept running by a few of the same people who once did the same for Paul Allen.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

by Kurt Schlosser on Nov 24, 2026 at 11:08 amNovember 25, 2026 at 8:16 am.

When Seattle’s Living Computers: Museum + Labs closed for good in 2024, it seemed like the end of the line for anyone who wanted to do more than just look at old computers.

But in a Tukwila business park 20 minutes south of downtown, a sizable collection of vintage computers is still alive — kept running by a few of the same people who once did the same for Paul Allen.

The Interim Computer Museum is a nonprofit that opened to the public in 2024 and has quietly grown into a hands-on showcase of dozens of machines, from early Apples and IBM PCs to hulking DEC systems that once filled university labs. At 4,400 square feet of public space, it’s nearly as significant as Living Computers was before that museum expanded in 2016.

ICM is led by Stephen Jones, who calls himself the museum’s “caretaker.” Jones spent two decades helping track down and restore machines for Allen, first at PDP Planet, Allen’s private collection of vintage systems, then at Living Computers, where he was senior engineering manager.

In a recent development, when the late Microsoft co-founder’s estate wound down Living Computers, the majority of the collection went to the Mimms Museum of Technology and Art in Georgia, where Jones is also a curator. The machines in Tukwila are privately owned, and Jones has helped bankroll ICM with personal funds, with prepares to eventually donate the collection to the nonprofit.

The Mimms museum now holds the Living Computers trademark and has granted ICM “legacy use” of the name, but Jones remarked he didn’t want to revive it as ICM’s own because “it has a finite past.” Instead, he wants to carry on “the spirit of the engineering focus.”.

“Between Mimms and here, this is the legacy,” Jones remarked. “We show the name and the connection to the past, but we’re doing latest things.”.

According to recent reports, ICM occupies space in Seattle Exchange @ Southcenter, a sprawl of low-slung flex buildings off Strander Boulevard near Westfield Southcenter mall. Its neighbors include a car detailer, a pest control organization, a welding shop, an embroiderer and an upholsterer.

Recent findings suggest that more than four decades ago, Seattle Computer Products operated just down Industry Drive. That’s where Tim Paterson wrote 86-DOS, the operating system Microsoft bought and turned into MS-DOS for IBM’s first PC.

Industry observers note that jones calls that proximity part of the “magic” of the location. The museum has a Gazelle computer that SCP built nearby, using boards that Jones noted the tech giant hired high school students to assemble and test. Volunteers recently pulled data off its hard drive, which boots into MS-DOS 2.11 and still holds SCP’s own source code.

Industry observers note that allen’s fingerprints are everywhere. One display holds a 1971 letter from Hellmut Golde, director of the University of Washington’s Computer Science Laboratory, kicking Allen and his “friends from the Lakeside School” out of the lab. Among the offenses: tying up the teletypes to print “endless listings,” and taking an acoustic coupler from a professor’s office “without leaving at least a note.” Golde asked them to turn in their keys.

In a recent development, the letter sits beside an Imlac PDS-1, the same type of graphics computer Golde scolded the teens for using without permission. More than five decades later, the letter is headed back to campus: ICM plans to display it, along with the Imlac, at UW’s 60th anniversary celebration for its computer science program in March.

Recent findings suggest that jones recalled that Allen insisted visitors to Living Computers get “the 10-minute experience” of loading an Altair 8800 from paper tape, just as he remembered it. The kit computer was the machine for which Allen and Bill Gates wrote Microsoft’s first product, and Allen wanted to reinforce “how far we’ve come and how difficult old computers were.” ICM has an Altair 8800 on display.

Around the corner is Miss Piggy, a DEC datasystem 570 that Microsoft used in the early 1980s to support the group that built Multiplan, Word and later Excel. It was also the email host for much of the firm, including Gates, who once had to print out an important message on its console printer when the system went down before a speaking engagement.

Recovered email highlights Allen pushing to get Piggy networked. “Paul Allen is very keen on doing this,” Henry Burgess wrote in 1982. Retired in 1986, the machine now runs again in Tukwila. It’s one of ICM’s most popular remote systems, and some fans come in just to write programs while sitting next to it.

Other local ties include a PDP-7 that Boeing used to process flight data in the 1960s, and a Toad-1, a modern take on the PDP-10 built in the 1990s by Redmond’s XKL. Jones first got involved with Allen’s world through a 1997 Usenet post inviting PDP-10 enthusiasts onto a Toad. That machine became the cornerstone of PDP Planet.

In a 2024 video for Christie’s, Jones said what inspired Allen was “being able to recover old programs, mythical code, and get them running on hardware so that they can be studied.”.

Sources indicate that asked what Allen would make of ICM, Jones didn’t hesitate. “I think he’d be happy,” he said.

On a monitor beside ICM’s PDP-6, a 1968 artificial intelligence program is having trouble.

“SORRY, I DON’T KNOW THE WORD ‘STEEPLE,'” it replies.

The program is SHRDLU, created by Terry Winograd at the MIT AI Lab. It let a user type plain-English commands to move blocks around a virtual world. Only the PDP-6’s front console and display survived, so ICM is rebuilding the machine as a “hybrid,” with the original hardware wired to an emulator.

Sources indicate that jones sees a lesson in that old error message. “You look at this and you think of how we use ChatGPT now,” he remarked. “The cool thing about SHRDLU is that it can tell you ‘I don’t know.’ It doesn’t try to fabricate anything.”.

ICM has its own ties to the modern AI world. An Anthropic employee is a member and strong supporter, and in October the museum brought six vintage computing stations to an Anthropic event, where the company’s Claude chatbot wrote programs for machines like the Commodore 64.

Back in Tukwila, Claude has become one of ICM’s most useful restoration tools. The team feeds it huge stacks of scanned documentation, such as the full set of schematics for a PDP-10. When a machine has a logic fault, they ask where to look, and Claude points them to a page in the maintenance manual or a likely bad module.

“That’s turned things that would take a couple of weeks to solve into a couple of days,” Jones said.

Sources indicate that AI can point the way, but the repairs remain hands-on work. When Miss Piggy wouldn’t run properly this year, former Living Computers engineer Josh Dersch stepped through the machine’s microcode one instruction at a time using a recreated DEC test board, until he found a single bad chip. A spare board brought it back.

Asked if it still takes a human to keep these machines running, Jones agreed — at least for now. If a humanoid robot with AI built in ever demonstrates up to do the repairs, he joked, “then I sit at the front desk all day.”.

Nearly everything at ICM is meant to be touched, switched on and played with, and that can be intimidating. On machines with nothing but a text prompt, “you kind of have to know the commands in your head already,” Jones noted.

That’s by design. From the start, the idea was to challenge people “either by confronting them with their past or demonstrating how difficult it was,” Jones said. His example: two friends, one with an Apple IIe and one with an IBM PC, whose computers “could never share” software. ICM continues that legacy, he said, “challenging the visitor to go beyond what they might feel comfortable with.”.

Industry observers note that volunteers have written cheat sheets to help newcomers, and Jones is encouraged when families come in and kids start typing BASIC programs. “That to me was the spirit of what PDP Planet and Living Computers was meant to be,” he noted.

Very little is behind glass. Jones jokes that a Timex Sinclair 1000, which would wipe your painstakingly typed program if you bumped it, is “the only computer that deserves to be behind glass.” The goal, he noted, is to avoid “a boneyard that people walk through.”.

Other highlights include Galaxy Game, the first coin-operated video game, installed at Stanford in 1971 and now being restored, and a Thinking Machines CM-2 supercomputer, whose 40th anniversary ICM just celebrated with members of its original design team.

Sources indicate that for younger engineers raised on modern tools, Jones has a go-to move. He asks if they’ve used Linux, then walks them over to the PDP-7, the type of machine Unix was first written on more than 50 years ago. Many of the basic commands they type every day started there.

That remote access helps explain why ICM has about 500 members and sponsors, even though only 81 members have visited in person this year. Memberships start at $36 a year. Along with a King County grant through 4Culture, they help cover rent, with personal funds from Jones filling the gap. The museum hopes to become self-sustaining within five years, and maybe someday buy its own building.

In a recent development, the museum’s name reflects the urgency. “We’re in this magic window right now, where the hardware can still run, we can still maintain it, you can replace parts,” Jones said. “But slowly we’re getting further and further away.”.

In a recent development, ICM is open Saturdays through Mondays from 10 a.m. to 4 p.m. Admission is $9 for adults and free for those under 18. Last May, the museum revived Vintage Computer Festival Pacific Northwest, which had been canceled in March 2020. The event drew 981 people, and it returns May 1–2 at the Tukwila Community Center.

Among the machines on the floor is MIT-AI, a DECsystem-2020 that once served as the ARPANET host for MIT’s Artificial Intelligence Lab. As Living Computers shut down in 2024, Christopher Zach, who sold the machine to Allen, told GeekWire he was ready to drive a U-Haul to Seattle to rescue it.

When a friend of Zach’s stopped by ICM’s booth at WorldCon and asked about “Chris’s computer,” Jones had a simple message to pass along: “Please just tell him it’s safe.”.

How to Finance Your Business’s Next Stage of Growth

📅 27 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (971 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Entrepreneur

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Opinions expressed by Entrepreneur contributors are their own.
  • Growth can create a real challenge for business leaders.
  • According to recent reports, in my role in senior financial leadership, I’ve learned that financing decisions involve both accessing capital and thoughtful strategy.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Opinions expressed by Entrepreneur contributors are their own.

Growth can create a real challenge for business leaders. The more successful a company becomes, the more capital it may require to keep growing and maintain or build on that level of success. Newly introduced customers demand inventory; additional capacity requires equipment; product innovation and expansion into new markets often involve substantial investment before new revenue is realized.

According to recent reports, in my role in senior financial leadership, I’ve learned that financing decisions involve both accessing capital and thoughtful strategy. These decisions shape a company’s financial obligations, ownership structure and ability to pursue future opportunities. These decisions also shape the operating model of the company and the future trajectory of the business.

Recent findings suggest that the challenge for companies experiencing growth is determining which combination of internal cash, debt and equity best supports the organization’s long-term ambitions. Any decision about capital strategy incorporates tradeoffs.

Before pursuing external financing, leadership teams should examine how effectively their operations generate and retain cash. Improving collections, managing inventory and reinvesting profits can fund expansion without increasing debt or diluting ownership. Many companies leverage a portion of self-financing as a larger part of their capitalization strategy, even a small portion included in a larger debt or equity stake.

According to recent reports, mailchimp demonstrated the potential of this approach, growing without outside equity financing before its acquisition by Intuit in a transaction valued at approximately $12 billion in 2021. Famously, Mailchimp avoided venture capital by prioritizing cash flow and streamlining operations to avoid needing outside capital. In 2020 and 2021, Mailchimp was pushing roughly $300 million in EBITDA.

According to recent reports, self-financing, however, is not equally practical across all industries. A software organization with recurring revenue and modest infrastructure requirements has a different capital demand than a manufacturer purchasing machinery or a transportation company expanding its fleet. For asset-heavy businesses, relying exclusively on internal cash may constrain growth and allow competitors to capture emerging opportunities.

The goal is to maximize internal funding while preserving sufficient liquidity to withstand unexpected expenses, delayed payments and economic uncertainty.

Recent findings suggest that debt and equity represent fundamentally different approaches to financing expansion. Debt creates contractual repayment obligations, while equity exchanges ownership for capital without conventional repayment requirements. Neither approach is better than the other, across the board. Their suitability as financing options depends on the predictability of cash flows, the risks associated with expansion and the company’s long-term objectives.

In equipment finance, financing income-producing assets requires balancing borrowing costs, repayment schedules and anticipated returns. Credit decisions are partially based on these business fundamentals. The same principle applies to businesses investing in production equipment, facilities and other revenue-generating assets. When cash flows are predictable, borrowing can allow owners to retain equity while capturing the financial benefits of expansion. Companies should also recognize that repayment obligations remain even when growth underperforms, potentially restricting liquidity and operational flexibility.

Equity offers an alternative approach for companies developing latest technologies, entering uncertain markets or pursuing investments with unpredictable near-term returns. Investors share financial risk and may contribute valuable expertise and connections, but their capital comes at the expense of future ownership and profits. A founder selling 20% of a business may obtain the financing needed to accelerate growth while trading a portion of eventual value.

According to recent reports, investors may also negotiate governance rights, just as lenders may impose financial covenants, something I have considerable experience with in my role as a CFO. Consequently, the true cost of capital extends beyond interest rates and valuation to include the strategic flexibility a manufacturer retains. Sometimes, a captive business interest by an individual or institution through equity can supercharge a business through ongoing partnership.

Whether a business is considering relying on cash flow for growth, debt financing or trading equity for capital, the business should consider how much capital the company needs and on what timeline.

An established distributor with predictable demand may use a revolving credit line to finance inventory and receivables, while a organization developing an innovative product may require equity to support years of research and market development, like in the biotech industry. In fact, biotech companies can require several years of clinical trial stage development, requiring massive cash runways prior to even conceiving going to market; many of these companies involve acquisitions or exits at maturity.

Many businesses benefit from combining financing sources, using retained earnings for operational improvements, borrowing for established revenue-generating activities and reserving equity for investments involving greater uncertainty.

Capital structures should support corporate strategy rather than dictate it. Businesses should recognize the challenges of dilution and not seek to raise too much capital. The objective is to fund what needs to be funded. The financing strategy that allows the company to pursue growth, withstand setbacks and preserve its ability to create long-term value is the ideal approach for a company making a decision about financing growth.

Growth can create a real challenge for business leaders. The more successful a firm becomes, the more capital it may require to keep growing and maintain or build on that level of success. Fresh customers demand inventory; additional capacity requires equipment; product innovation and expansion into new markets often involve substantial investment before new revenue is realized.

It has been revealed that in my role in senior financial leadership, I’ve learned that financing decisions involve both accessing capital and thoughtful strategy. These decisions shape a company’s financial obligations, ownership structure and ability to pursue future opportunities. These decisions also shape the operating model of the company and the future trajectory of the business.

Industry observers note that the challenge for companies experiencing growth is determining which combination of internal cash, debt and equity best supports the company’s long-term ambitions. Any decision about capital strategy incorporates tradeoffs.

#169102. Stop Building AI Into Your Product. Let Your Customers Bring Their Own.

📅 27 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1450 w)
📖 Baca
AI & Tech ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Entrepreneur ↗ Open Full Page

Stop Building AI Into Your Product. Let Your Customers Bring Their Own.

📅 27 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1450 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Entrepreneur

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Opinions expressed by Entrepreneur contributors are their own.
  • In a recent development, over the past two years, almost every software manufacturer has felt the same pressure: Add AI to the product, or look outdated.
  • Sources indicate that I run a tech giant that makes help desk software for businesses, and we went through this too.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Opinions expressed by Entrepreneur contributors are their own.

In a recent development, over the past two years, almost every software manufacturer has felt the same pressure: Add AI to the product, or look outdated. So we all did. Chat panels appeared in the corner of every dashboard. “Summarize with AI” buttons revealed up next to every text field. Pricing pages grew a fresh line item for AI credits.

Sources indicate that I run a tech giant that makes help desk software for businesses, and we went through this too. But somewhere along the way, I noticed something about our customers that changed how I think about the whole question.

If you sell to businesses, look at what your customers’ employees have open on their screens. Very often it’s a corporate Claude or ChatGPT subscription, or Microsoft 365 Copilot bundled into the Office licenses the tech giant was paying for anyway. Someone in IT or finance evaluated it, signed a contract, went through a security review and rolled it out.

According to recent reports, that assistant is becoming the company’s “at-home AI.” It’s the one employees are trained on, the one legal has approved, and increasingly, the one that has context about the business: documents, email, meeting notes, internal wikis. Every company will have one eventually. Frankly, most already do.

It has been revealed that now imagine that same company uses eight or 10 business tools, and each of those vendors has bolted on its own AI assistant. Each one has a different interface, different limits and different data policies. None of them know what the others know. The help desk AI has no idea what was discussed in the CRM, and the CRM’s AI can’t see the project tracker.

Sources indicate that that’s not a better workplace. It’s AI sprawl, and it’s the opposite of what the customer wants.

In a recent development, the alternative is simple: Instead of building an assistant into your product, make your product easy for the customer’s existing assistant to use. Let them bring their own agent.

If that phrase sounds familiar, it should. A decade ago, “bring your own device” (BYOD) changed how companies thought about laptops and phones. More recently, “bring your own key” (BYOK) let customers plug their own AI provider’s API key into software instead of paying the vendor for AI usage. Bring your own agent (BYOA) is the next step: The customer doesn’t just bring the key; they bring the whole assistant, with its context, its permissions and its security approvals already in place.

Recent findings suggest that for the customer, the benefits are obvious. They use a tool they already pay for and already know. Their assistant can combine data from your product with everything else it has access to. Asking “which of our biggest accounts filed support tickets this week, and what did we promise them in the last renewal call?” only works if one assistant can see both the help desk and the meeting notes.

For the vendor, the benefits are less obvious but just as real.

You stay out of the token-reselling business: When you build AI features on top of a model provider, you’re effectively buying compute wholesale and reselling it. Your costs grow with usage, your margins depend on someone else’s pricing changes, and you end up designing credit systems and usage caps instead of building your actual product. With BYOA, the customer’s AI subscription covers the compute. Your product provides the data and the actions.

Industry observers note that you stop competing with companies that spend billions on models: No software vendor of normal size is going to build a better general-purpose assistant than the frontier AI labs. Trying to match them feature for feature is a losing race. Being the best tool their assistant can connect to is a race you can actually win.

It clarifies product decisions: This one surprised me the most. Once you accept that the customer’s assistant will handle the conversation, the question shifts from “What AI features should we build?” to “What can our product do, and how cleanly can we expose it?” That’s a much healthier question. It pushes you to make your core functionality solid, well-structured and well-permissioned, which is good for every user, not just the ones using AI.

Recent findings suggest that it’s a marketing channel, too: This is the least obvious benefit. AI clients now have their own connector directories, and there’s a growing number of independent MCP registries and listing sites. Getting listed puts your product in front of people at the exact moment they’re looking for tools to connect to their assistant. It’s a new distribution channel, it’s still relatively uncrowded, and it costs you nothing beyond the integration you were building anyway.

According to recent reports, this doesn’t mean built-in AI has no place. Some features, such as automatic ticket categorization that runs in the background without anyone asking, make sense to keep inside the product. But the conversational assistant, the one people talk to, increasingly belongs to the customer, not to you.

According to recent reports, the practical way to do this today is to implement an MCP server for your product. MCP, the Model Context Protocol, is an open standard that lets AI assistants discover and use tools in external applications. It’s supported by Claude, ChatGPT, Microsoft Copilot Studio and a growing list of other clients. You describe what your product can do, such as search records, create items or update statuses, and any compatible assistant can use those actions on the user’s behalf, within that user’s existing permissions.

There are two common ways to ship an MCP server, and the choice matters more than it seems.

It has been revealed that 1. A hosted endpoint over HTTP: Your product exposes an MCP endpoint on its own servers, using the protocol’s streamable HTTP transport. The customer adds a URL to their assistant, signs in, and that’s it. Nothing gets installed. When you add new capabilities or fix a bug, every customer gets the update immediately, because there’s only one version: the one you’re running.

2. A local package. You publish a command-line tool or npm package that runs on the user’s machine and talks to your API. This was the common approach early on, and it still works for individual developers.

I strongly recommend the first option. We started with both at my firm, and we’re now phasing out the local package. Each installed copy is a version you can’t update, and customers running old packages kept missing newer features.

Industry observers note that but the bigger reason is security. Large organizations increasingly won’t allow third-party code to run on employee machines, and for good reason. The past couple of years have brought a steady stream of critical-severity vulnerabilities and software supply chain attacks, including compromised packages in the npm ecosystem itself. Asking a security team to approve a package that runs locally with access to firm data is a hard sell. Asking them to approve an HTTPS endpoint on a vendor they’ve already vetted is a much easier conversation.

According to recent reports, A hosted endpoint also fits how companies roll out AI. Organization-wide connectors in enterprise AI prepares are typically set up once by an administrator and then made available to everyone. Support OAuth sign-in so each employee connects with their own account and permissions, and you’ve removed most of the friction.

In a recent development, it’s tempting to view the customer’s AI assistant as a competitor for attention. If people spend their day in Claude or Copilot, won’t they spend less time in your product?

It has been revealed that maybe. But they were going to use that assistant anyway. The real question is whether it can reach your product when they need it. If it can’t, you’re the tool that gets worked around. If it can, you’re part of how the company works.

B2B buyers don’t want another AI. They want the one they already have to work with everything else they pay for. Build for that.

According to recent reports, over the past two years, almost every software company has felt the same pressure: Add AI to the product, or look outdated. So we all did. Chat panels appeared in the corner of every dashboard. “Summarize with AI” buttons revealed up next to every text field. Pricing pages grew a newly introduced line item for AI credits.

In a recent development, I run a firm that makes help desk software for businesses, and we went through this too. But somewhere along the way, I noticed something about our customers that changed how I think about the whole question.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • by Kurt Schlosser on Nov 24, 2026 at 1:27 pmNovember 24, 2026 at 2:04 pm.
  • Sources indicate that A billboard taking a swipe at Anthropic’s Claude might sound like the work of a rival AI company.
  • “The only Claude you need is Monet,” the sign reads.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

by Kurt Schlosser on Nov 24, 2026 at 1:27 pmNovember 24, 2026 at 2:04 pm.

Sources indicate that A billboard taking a swipe at Anthropic’s Claude might sound like the work of a rival AI company. This one is from the Seattle Art Museum.

“The only Claude you need is Monet,” the sign reads. It’s part of the latest wave of messages in SAM’s “Dear Seattle” campaign, which has spent the fall urging people to look up from their screens and see something in person.

Earlier billboards around the city told passersby to “come stare at something that isn’t your inbox” and noted that “even the algorithm thinks you should get out more.” The final batch pushes the AI jokes further, including one asking for “a little more art and a little less artificial” and another promising, “Your phone doesn’t have to know.”.

Tech billboards are a fixture in the San Francisco Bay Area, where AI startups cover Highway 101 and city streets with ads that often mean little to anyone outside the industry.

They’re less common around Seattle. Anthropic put up a big orange Claude billboard over Aurora Avenue in 2024, and this spring Bellevue startup Summation put one up along SR 520 because “startup energy should be more visible around here,” its CEO told GeekWire.

“In a city where so much of our lives happens on screens, we’re making a playful case for the things you can only experience in person,” Kat Bryant Flaherty, SAM’s director of communications, mentioned in a statement. She listed “the scale and texture of an artwork, a film with a room full of strangers, making something with your hands, or catching up with a friend over a meal.”.

The campaign is tied to changes at the downtown museum itself, where SAM is adding more public space and more reasons to linger, including hands-on art making and music in the Studio at SAM and the newly opened Bar Dojo restaurant.

The campaign runs through the end of the year, with more than 200 ads across the region — more than 20 billboards plus spots on light rail and digital kiosks.

SAM’s campaign is about the same size as the one Bellevue startup Statsig ran in the Bay Area in 2024, with more than 200 billboards and transit posters, but pointed in the opposite direction.

SAM is offering buy-one-get-one-free tickets in December with the code “LOVESAM,” good at both the downtown museum and the Seattle Asian Art Museum in Volunteer Park, to encourage people to visit together.

“We’re hoping to grab attention, spark curiosity, and remind Seattle that there’s a lot happening at SAM worth leaving the house for,” Flaherty said.

#169099. FinCEN Bars US Institutions From Transmitting Funds to MEXC: What Changes and What Doesn't

📅 07 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 8m • 📚 Deep Dive (1580 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Nulltx ↗ Open Full Page

FinCEN Bars US Institutions From Transmitting Funds to MEXC: What Changes and What Doesn't

📅 07 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1580 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Nulltx

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that finCEN's November 6 order cuts US financial institutions off from MEXC Global, barring any transmittal of funds to or from the exchange.
  • MEXC states user assets remain secure.
  • On November 6, the Financial Crimes Enforcement Network issued a final order under Section 9714(a) of the Combating Russian Money Laundering Act.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

AI-assisted summary, reviewed by NullTX editors.

Sources indicate that finCEN's November 6 order cuts US financial institutions off from MEXC Global, barring any transmittal of funds to or from the exchange. The order spells out what is banned, what MEXC is accused of, and how the exchange has answered.

MEXC states user assets remain secure. The FinCEN order never suggested otherwise, and the gap between the exchange's reassurance and the order's actual target is the key to this story.

On November 6, the Financial Crimes Enforcement Network issued a final order under Section 9714(a) of the Combating Russian Money Laundering Act. It names MEXC Global a financial institution of primary money laundering concern in connection with Russian illicit finance. From there, it bars "covered financial institutions," a category that includes banks, broker-dealers and money transmitters, from any transmittal of funds to or from MEXC Global. Transmittals, as defined, include convertible virtual currency.

It has been revealed that on the MEXC side, the reach is wide. The order covers the exchange's subsidiaries, branches and offices outside the United States: MEXC Global Ltd and MX Global Ltd in Seychelles, MEXC Estonia OÜ, GIDA Technology AG in Switzerland and MXC Global Ltd in the United Kingdom. Former Singapore entities and any successors are included as well. US-based affiliates, by contrast, are expressly excluded.

According to recent reports, the ban won't bite right away. It takes effect 30 days after publication in the Federal Register, which had not happened as of the announcement, and it carries no end date. FinCEN keeps the authority to attach conditions and grant exemptions, and willful violations can lead to civil and criminal penalties under 31 U.S.C. 5321 and 5322.

MEXC's statement is short and carefully built. The exchange says it is aware of the order and is reviewing it with its legal and compliance teams. It describes itself as operating normally, with user assets secure. It also says it takes the concerns seriously, plans to engage constructively with FinCEN and other regulators, and has started an independent review of its AML and sanctions controls.

Two points stand out. For one, the reassurance lines up with the order's text. Nothing in it freezes balances or halts trading, so "operating normally" is plausible. The threat is to MEXC's access to US financial counterparties, not to the exchange's wallets.

According to recent reports, the other point is what the statement skips. It disputes none of the allegations, and the independent review it promises targets AML and sanctions controls, the very area where FinCEN says the exchange failed. The order also invites anyone with relevant information to submit it to FinCEN, so MEXC already has a formal channel for the constructive engagement it describes.

The charges are specific. FinCEN assesses that MEXC facilitated at least $16.7 billion in likely illicit activity between May 2021 and May 2026, a figure Treasury's announcement rounded to $16 billion. The order splits that total across several categories.

On Russia, FinCEN cites nearly $1.5 billion in direct and indirect exposure to sanctions-evasion transactions, including $232 million in direct dealings with entities sanctioned by the US, EU or UK. According to the order, MEXC processed about $129 million with Garantex and $4.1 million with its successor Grinex after both were designated, with activity continuing as recently as June 2026. It also points to at least $26 million benefiting the A7 Network and nearly $200 million tied to the ruble-backed A7A5 token. Beyond that, FinCEN says MEXC handled more than $13 billion with four UK-sanctioned exchanges between May 2018 and July 2026.

Iran features just as heavily. The order cites nearly $2 billion tied to Iranian actors or terrorist groups, including about $1.87 billion in exposure to Iran and over $1 billion in direct transactions with more than 40 Iranian exchanges. About $22 million is linked to the Central Bank of Iran and the IRGC Quds Force. For North Korea, the order describes roughly $350,000 received by a sanctioned money launderer between June and September 2025. On cybercrime, it cites $1.99 billion in flows linked to illicit cyber actors and $37.9 million in suspected ransomware payments between January 2022 and July 2024.

The order then turns to MEXC's own rulebook. Its stated KYC and AML policies prohibit accounts in certain jurisdictions, yet FinCEN claims the exchange facilitated transactions involving them. The order also notes that MEXC has operated without a license in Seychelles, Hong Kong and Japan, and it points to the Seychelles Financial Services Authority's May 2026 enforcement action against MX Global Ltd. All of this reflects FinCEN's assessments, drawn from public and non-public information, and MEXC has not answered them point by point.

The order is not an OFAC sanctions designation, and the difference matters. A funds-transmittal ban limits what US-covered institutions can do with MEXC. It does not make it illegal for ordinary consumers anywhere in the world to hold an account there. The order also states that it leaves existing Bank Secrecy Act and OFAC obligations untouched.

Industry observers note that section 9714 gives Treasury two routes: the special measures of Section 311 of the USA PATRIOT Act, or a ban on certain transmittals of funds. FinCEN took the second and explained its reasoning. Recordkeeping requirements would still let transfers continue, and a correspondent-account restriction would miss funds moving outside a strict correspondent relationship. FinCEN also went with an order rather than a rulemaking, citing imminent threats and ongoing transactions.

One provision stands out for its practicality. FinCEN acknowledges that a covered institution often can't reject incoming crypto before it arrives, so the order allows discretion in cases such as funds that sat in an unhosted wallet for an extended period. The carve-out underlines how difficult enforcement will be in practice.

For most MEXC customers outside the US, nothing changes on day one. Counterparties face a tougher picture. Once the order takes effect, US banks, regulated exchanges and money transmitters will have to block transmittals to and from MEXC, and global institutions with US exposure have strong reasons to follow suit. FinCEN indicates plainly that the order puts US and foreign financial institutions and regulators on notice.

Before issuance, the draft went to the Justice Department, State, the Federal Reserve, the FDIC, the SEC, the CFTC, the OCC and the NCUA, and none objected. The order also fits into a wider Treasury campaign. It cites the October 1 Operation Economic Outcast action against the A7 Network, and a separate FinCEN proposal on A7 sub-agents followed days later.

Recent findings suggest that predicting how consumers or markets will react would be guesswork. What users can do is track the dates, know which institutions they depend on, and watch for official updates from MEXC.

In a recent development, finCEN used the same Section 9714 authority against the exchange Bitzlato in January 2023. This time, though, the target is by FinCEN's own account among the 20 largest exchanges by trading volume, with roughly 9% of centralized exchange market share as of December 2025 and about $5 billion in reserve assets as of June 2026. Applying a transmittal ban to an exchange of that size signals a more aggressive posture.

Three things will show what comes next. The first is the Federal Register publication date, which starts the 30-day clock. The second is whether FinCEN grants any exemptions or conditions. The third is what MEXC's independent review turns up, and whether the exchange shares the results. For now, the statement buys MEXC time without answering the order. The real answer will come from changes to its controls, and from whether its banking and liquidity partners are satisfied with them.
