Amazon discriminated against Iranian job candidate under global hiring policy, Ontario tribunal rules

📅 27 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (787 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Geekwire

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • by Todd Bishop on Nov 27, 2026 at 2:21 pmNovember 27, 2026 at 2:21 pm.
  • An Ontario human rights tribunal ruled that Amazon violated provincial law when it dropped a Toronto software engineer from its hiring process because of his Iranian citizenship.
  • The company’s internal policy, applied worldwide, barred some Iranian citizens from jobs involving access to Amazon’s encrypted technology, according to the ruling.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

by Todd Bishop on Nov 27, 2026 at 2:21 pmNovember 27, 2026 at 2:21 pm.

An Ontario human rights tribunal ruled that Amazon violated provincial law when it dropped a Toronto software engineer from its hiring process because of his Iranian citizenship.

The company’s internal policy, applied worldwide, barred some Iranian citizens from jobs involving access to Amazon’s encrypted technology, according to the ruling.

In a Nov. 16 decision, the Human Rights Tribunal of Ontario ordered Amazon to pay 15,000 Canadian dollars (about US$10,500) plus interest to Mohammadhasan Owlia, whose hiring process it ended in 2020. The tribunal rejected Amazon’s argument that U.S. export controls required the policy.

Export controls are U.S. rules that limit who can get access to certain American technology, including some encryption software.

The tribunal found that Amazon never indicated that the mid-level software engineering job for which Owlia applied would have involved any restricted technology. Expert witnesses for both sides agreed that the U.S. rules don’t ban hiring Iranian citizens, though a company may need a government license before giving them access to certain technology.

“Stated simply, Amazon’s export controls compliance policy was overbroad,” wrote Cyndee Todgham Cherniak, the tribunal vice-chair who decided the case.

Amazon stated in a statement to Canadian news outlets that it is committed to “fair and inclusive hiring and to following the laws wherever we operate, including Ontario’s Human Rights Code,” and that it will review the decision and meet its obligations under it.

The ruling was reported earlier by the Toronto Star and the Globe and Mail. We’ve asked Amazon whether the policy remains in effect elsewhere, including in the U.S.

Owlia, a University of Toronto engineering graduate who held an open work permit allowing him to work in Canada, applied for the job in 2019 and passed Amazon’s online technical assessment. On a pre-interview call in January 2020, a recruiter noticed he had studied in Tehran and told him Amazon had a policy against hiring Iranians.

Amazon’s guide for recruiters, quoted in the decision, says to end the process in those cases and tell candidates only that the organization “has decided to not move forward with the hiring process.”.

It has been revealed that the policy, as quoted in the decision, also covers citizens of Cuba, North Korea, Sudan and Syria. It covers candidates, employees, temporary workers and contractors with access to Amazon’s encrypted technology, except lower-level warehouse jobs. It applies globally, but it exempts U.S. citizens, U.S. permanent residents, refugees, people granted asylum, and anyone whose most recent citizenship or permanent residency is from a country not on the list.

Owlia’s lawyers noted that an Amazon recruitment manager acknowledged during cross-examination that the policy remained in effect, according to the ruling. She also testified that Owlia would have been eligible once he became a Canadian permanent resident in 2021.

The tribunal’s orders apply only to hiring in Ontario by Amazon Fulfillment Services ULC, the Canadian subsidiary named in the case. Within six months, Amazon must revise the policy and the recruiter guide to require compliance with Ontario’s Human Rights Code there, and its Ontario-based HR staff must take human rights training.

The tribunal declined to award about C$92,500 (about US$65,000) in lost wages, calling the claim too speculative.

“In my view, having to comply with multiple laws is a cost of doing business,” Todgham Cherniak wrote.

Recent findings suggest that in the U.S., the Immigration and Nationality Act protects U.S. citizens and nationals, eligible permanent residents, refugees and people granted asylum from hiring discrimination based on citizenship status. Workers on temporary visas generally fall outside that specific protection. The Justice Department has warned employers that screening out applicants from particular countries can still amount to national origin discrimination.

The U.S. Commerce Department indicates that giving Iranian nationals access to controlled technology or certain software can require a license, including when the transfer happens in the U.S. or a third country.

It has been revealed that A similar dispute surfaced at Booking.com in 2022, when the company canceled the employment contracts of 11 Iranian hires living in Iran just before they were due to start at its Amsterdam headquarters. Booking.com cited complications in hiring and relocating them and said the move had nothing to do with discrimination, Skift reported. An internal document cited a possible “sanction risk” in employing Iranian residents, according to NL Times.

“I’m proud that I stood up for my right to be judged on my ability to do the work, instead of where my birth certificate was issued,” Owlia noted in a statement released by his lawyers at Toronto firm Kastner Ko.

Owlia is now a Canadian citizen and an engineering manager at a Toronto software startup.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that chan Park feels like “an eternal nomad.” He has since age 12, when he moved from Korea to the U.S., where he attended middle school in Minnesota, followed by high school in New Jersey, followed by college in New Hampshire. Then he really began to bounce around. Park worked as a trader in New York out of college, embraced the ski-bum life in Utah, then headed to Asia for Uber, where he spent six years, running its expansion team, then managing its entire Southeast Asia business out of Singapore.

It has been revealed that more specifically, he was responsible for eight countries across the region, and 350 people, which didn’t give him a lot of time to organize his home. But he wasn’t overwhelmed by the chaos. Instead, he states that in Singapore, something unusual happened. “There’s this huge culture of landlords furnishing space to attract expats,” explains Park. “The furnishings aren’t super high-end, but they’re well-designed and well put together, and it enabled me to be basically moved in as soon as I put my clothes in the closet.” Suddenly, coming home was a treat — a new sensation for him. “For the first time, I was proud to host friends for dinners and barbecues and to just open the door and relax.”.

Park knew his U.S. friends could benefit from the same experience, and before long, he was talking with his Dartmouth classmate turned product and industrial designer Christian Talmage about forming their own company. Enter Oliver Space, which provides a lot of what that Singaporean landlord delivered to Park. It furnishes places for busy professionals, making moving into a latest home as easy as hanging up their clothes.

The now year-old service is available in the Bay Area only. And Oliver Space employs just a dozen people so far. But the company has already gained enough traction to attract $6.8 million in seed funding from an interesting array of investors, including Mayfield, Abstract Ventures, investors Jana Messerschmidt and April Underwood, Opendoor founder Eric Wu, and Kevin and Julia Hartz of Eventbrite, among others.

Now, Oliver Space just has to grow as promptly, or more so, than other furniture-as-service startups to recently attract funding.

Most Unicorns Are Worth More Than Their Last Funding-Round Valuations, Crunchbase Estimates

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The more than 1,900 startups on the The Crunchbase Unicorn Board have a combined valuation of roughly $9 trillion, based on their last reported valuations.
  • Most unicorns are estimated to have gained value, even as others have lost ground, our analysis shows.
  • According to recent reports, the majority of companies on the board are valued higher by the Current Valuations model than they were when they last raised funding.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The more than 1,900 startups on the The Crunchbase Unicorn Board have a combined valuation of roughly $9 trillion, based on their last reported valuations. But Crunchbase’s upcoming Current Valuation Model, which estimates how private-manufacturer values have changed since their last funding rounds, puts that figure closer to $11 trillion.

Most unicorns are estimated to have gained value, even as others have lost ground, our analysis shows. Among the biggest potential gainers are AI startups Thinking Machines Lab, whose estimated value has climbed from $12 billion to $40 billion, and Sierra, from nearly $16 billion to $31.5 billion.

According to recent reports, the majority of companies on the board are valued higher by the Current Valuations model than they were when they last raised funding. Only around 236 companies — roughly 12% of the board — are down by more than $100 million in value compared to their last reported valuations.

Industry observers note that the valuation model estimates that a select group of 24 companies have gained more than $10 billion in value since their most recent funding rounds. They include Mira Murati’s AI research lab Thinking Machines Lab, which was last valued at $12 billion in its 2025 seed funding but has a current valuation projected at $40 billion.

Industry observers note that similarly, Bret Taylor’s customer oriented AI agent builder Sierra was last valued at close to $16  billion in a May 2026 funding round. It is now estimated to be valued at $31.5 billion, per the Crunchbase model. (On Monday, Bloomberg reported that Sierra is raising a newly introduced round at a roughly $30 billion valuation.).

Physical Intelligence, a organization building AI for robotics, was valued at $5.6 billion in its Series B. Crunchbase’s Current Valuation model estimates its valuation now at $18.5 billion.

Another 53 companies are estimated to have current valuations that are $5 billion to just under $10 billion higher than those achieved in their most recent funding rounds. They include Unconventional AI, which is focused on energy efficiency for AI; Lila Sciences, which is building artificial intelligence for science; AI cloud company Vultr; AI research lab humans&; stablecoin payment platform Tempo; and Yann LeCun’s Advanced Machine Intelligence, which is modeling physical world intelligence.

In a recent development, A total of 484 companies are estimated to have current valuations that are $1 billion to $5 billion higher than their most recent funding valuations. More than 1,100 companies have values that were flat or up to $1 billion higher than their most recent funding valuations.

Only around 236 companies are estimated to be below their most recent valuation, by more than $100 million. Collectively, their current valuations are down by $326 billion from their most recent fundings, Crunchbase estimates.

According to recent reports, the Crunchbase Unicorn Board reached its highest value in 2026 as three companies approached or exceeded $1 trillion valuations — unprecedented in the board’s history. The board peaked at $10 trillion in advance of the Anthropic IPO this past week. The company’s public-market debut removed close to $1 trillion from the board. This followed another trillion-dollar exit from the board earlier this year, when SpaceX — last valued at $1.3 trillion in a secondary financing this year — before it went public in June at a value of $1.8 trillion.

In a recent development, all told, the unicorn board this year is at the moment up by $1.5 trillion from its $7.5 trillion value at the end of 2025. With its closest rival now on the public markets, OpenAI is currently the most highly valued private company at an official valuation of $1.25 trillion.

Sources indicate that the unicorn board has picked up pace this year. Around 360 companies joined the board so far this year, the second highest count in a single year after 2021 when 621 companies joined.

A faster pace of new entrants and rising valuations have helped replenish the board, while current estimates suggest substantial additional value has accumulated between funding rounds.

The next test is how closely these estimated values align with prices investors are willing to pay. Future funding rounds, secondary transactions, public listings and M&A will reveal how much of the board’s estimated $2 trillion uplift translates into realized value.

Industry observers note that current valuations are based on the upcoming Crunchbase Current Valuation Model, which prices companies using a proprietary machine learning model that starts with a firm’s most recent post-money valuation and continuously estimates how its value has shifted since that funding event. The model covers roughly 230,000 funded private companies. Read more here.

#169055. Five Forged Receipts Drained $304.5K From Ankr's Ethereum Bridge Using a 0.0044 ankrETH Deposit

📅 10 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (1050 w)
📖 Baca

Five Forged Receipts Drained $304.5K From Ankr's Ethereum Bridge Using a 0.0044 ankrETH Deposit

📅 10 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1050 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Nulltx

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that slowMist claims five forged receipts with valid signatures let an attacker drain about $304,500 from Ankr's Ethereum bridge using one old Optimism deposit.
  • On November 9, an attacker drained about $304,500 from Ankr's Ethereum cross-chain bridge.
  • All five carried valid signatures from the bridge's trusted consensus signer.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

AI-assisted summary, reviewed by NullTX editors.

Sources indicate that slowMist claims five forged receipts with valid signatures let an attacker drain about $304,500 from Ankr's Ethereum bridge using one old Optimism deposit. Here is how the check failed.Every one of the five receipts was signed by the bridge's own trusted signer. Every one pointed to a deposit that had already been paid out.

On November 9, an attacker drained about $304,500 from Ankr's Ethereum cross-chain bridge. According to SlowMist's alert, the attacker built five forged receipts that all referenced a single legitimate Optimism transaction, changing the recipient, the token and the withdrawal amount in each one.

All five carried valid signatures from the bridge's trusted consensus signer.

Sources indicate that the reused transaction was tiny: a deposit of about 0.0044 ankrETH made on Optimism on November 3, which SlowMist's analysis notes had already been redeemed on Ethereum the same day. Six days later, that one settled deposit was cited five times. The incident is recorded in the SlowMist Hacked database.Blockaid flagged the exploit as it unfolded, at about 08:42 UTC, with roughly $292,000 already gone. SlowMist followed at 09:14 UTC with the higher $304,500 estimate and an explanation of the forged receipts. Ankr paused withdrawals, and no recovery proposal has been confirmed.

The design is common across lock-and-release bridges. A user deposits on the source chain, and an off-chain set of signers watches for that deposit and signs a receipt describing it. The destination contract, in this case Ankr's Ethereum bridge contract, checks that the receipt carries a valid signature and then releases the funds.That setup makes the signers the source of truth. The contract can't see Optimism, so it leans on the signature to prove the deposit happened. The weak point sits in the gap between "the signer signed this" and "this really happened." A contract that treats the first as proof of the second inherits every mistake the signing process makes.

Recent findings suggest that the Ethereum transactions show the attacker extracted about 82.91 ankrETH, 515,206 ankrPOL and 7.98 million ANKR tokens. Blockaid described the five withdraw calls as using the tiny Optimism deposit to unlock the bridge's locked inventory and send it to a new wallet.The mix of assets tells its own story. Each forged receipt named a different token and amount, which suggests the attacker picked targets based on what the bridge held. That fits receipts built entirely by the attacker, apart from the one real transaction reference. Anyone wanting to trace them can open the bridge contract's transaction list on Etherscan and filter for the five `withdraw` calls on November 9.

Sources indicate that the most vital fact is still missing. SlowMist states the origin of the unauthorized signatures is under investigation, and it hasn't confirmed whether the signers were compromised.A valid signature on a forged receipt has a short list of explanations. A signing key, or the service holding it, could have been accessed. A signing service could have been tricked into signing attacker-supplied data. Or the signing logic itself could have a flaw that produces signatures for receipts it shouldn't. Each one points to a different fix: a stolen key means rotating signers, a manipulated service means tightening input validation off-chain, and a logic flaw means rewriting the signing rules.Whichever it turns out to be, the on-chain contract and the off-chain signer both failed to ask the same question. Either one verifying the source event would likely have stopped the attack, and neither did.

Recent findings suggest that the lessons are narrow and practical. Replay protection should key on the immutable identity of the source event, not on the receipt's contents, and a source event should be consumable exactly once. The destination contract should confirm that the receipt's recipient, token and amount match what the source-chain event actually recorded, using a proof or an independent verifier instead of trusting the signer alone.Signer infrastructure needs its own scrutiny. Threshold schemes, hardware-backed keys and strict limits on what a signing service will sign all shrink the damage from a single failure. Rate limits and per-withdrawal caps help as well. A bridge that can release its entire locked inventory in five calls has no brake once a signature check is defeated.Trust in a bridge comes in layers, and one layer rarely holds up alone. Consumers with funds in Ankr's bridge should watch for the project's post-mortem and its proposal for restoring withdrawals. For developers, the question to put to their own code is a blunt one: if a signer signs something false, what stops the contract from believing it?

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Delivery supply chains are the lifeblood of contemporary businesses — and a upcoming startup is betting that purpose-built AI agents can make them run a lot more smoothly.

Industry observers note that on Tuesday, Pedestal AI emerged from stealth with $4.7 million in seed funding. The company’s goal is to use agentic AI to make supply chains faster and more reliable — a proposal that’s already brought them together with Fortune 500 companies and some of the largest shipping firms in the world.

The seed round was led by Eclipse, with participation from RRE, Converge VC, Timescale Ventures, and VitalStage. Pedestal says the funding will be used to expand its product and engineering time, grow the marketing organization, and support additional deployments.

Recent findings suggest that in practice, much of Pedestal’s work is about removing friction from the shipping process — with agentic technology used as a means to that end. In one case, the company reduced missed deliveries for a major furniture company by 20% by deploying agents to take on some of the work that drivers were supposed to do. The agentic system they built would call customers 30 minutes before a delivery and collect any special instructions; if the call didn’t go through, a text would be sent from a separate system. Along the way, the deployment collected a wealth of data about friction points in the process, which could be used to optimize the system even further.

In a recent development, CEO Raj Aggarwal claims contemporary AI systems are particularly useful for dealing with that data. “The challenge is that the data is messy and it’s constantly changing,” Aggarwal told TechCrunch. “It’s disparate because it sits in so many legacy systems. That’s what makes it hard.”.

Supply chain AI has become a particularly hot space in recent months as alumni from autonomous driving teams look to launch their own startups. The supply chain startup Atomic, launched by a team of Tesla alumni, came out of stealth in 2025 with an emphasis on streamlining inventory. Another venture called Loop was launched by Uber alums to focus on predictive analytics.

As Aggarwal sees it, deliveries are particularly well-suited to training reinforcement learning systems. Because of their high volumes and easily measured outcomes, it’s easy to fine-tune contemporary AI systems toward what’s working and away from what isn’t.

Perhaps most importantly, it’s the kind of problem that can have an immediate effect on a client’s bottom line, making it easy to justify the expense.

“If you can get it right,” he told TechCrunch, “you can have really substantial impact.”.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

After a hacker stole customer data, Binance founder Changpeng Zhao advised 1Password consumers to change all the passwords stored in the service.

1Password offered different advice about what consumers should do after the incident was disclosed on Nov. 25. The password management service remarked hackers hadn't gained access to the passwords stored in users' vaults, so there was no need to reset them.

"If you use 1Password, recommend you to change ALL your passwords. It's a pain in the neck, but necessary," Zhao said on X, replying to a post from Coin Bureau about the breach.

If you have a crypto exchange login stored in 1Password, this distinction is important.

Scammers could still use the stolen email addresses to contact people they know are 1Password users.

1Password started investigating on Nov. 19 after detecting signs of possible unauthorized access to an employee's corporate GitHub account.

Industry observers note that from there, the hacker was able to steal private source code and inject malicious code into 1Password's backend services. The malicious code then downloaded certain administrative data about customers.

1Password publicly disclosed the breach on Nov. 25, six days later.

The tech giant did not specify how many customers were affected or explain exactly how the hacker managed to take over the employee's account.

The stolen data included customer names, login email addresses, account and user IDs, and timestamps indicating account creation and last use.

The hacker also gained access to 1Password's software development and deployment systems.

1Password disabled the compromised employee's GitHub account and revoked the stolen access token.

The company also restored a clean version of the affected service and revoked or replaced potentially exposed internal credentials.

1Password also engaged independent security experts to review its response.

1Password recommends that customers check the 1Password app or type the firm's website address directly into their browser if they receive an unexpected invitation or recovery message.

The tech giant states it will never contact users to request their account password or Secret Key.

Update: 1Password claims that there is no need to change one's 1Password account password or any of the passwords saved in one's vault. No customer passwords were exposed in this incident.

Hi CZ! There’s no need to change your 1Password account password or any of the passwords you’ve saved in your vault. No customer passwords were exposed in this incident. We don’t store your account password or Secret Key, and getting into our backend systems didn’t give the attacker the keys to decrypt your vault. The attacker did copy account information for some customers, including names and email addresses, so we recommend watching for 1Password invitations or account recovery emails you weren’t expecting. You can read the full update on our blog: https://t.co/9fbzzAJr0B.

#169051. Startups Are Picking Names That Can Work Even If The Original Business Model Doesn’t

📅 24 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (834 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Crunchbase ↗ Open Full Page

Startups Are Picking Names That Can Work Even If The Original Business Model Doesn’t

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (834 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Crunchbase

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Startup naming tends to be a cyclical endeavor.
  • Per a Crunchbase analysis of startups 1 founded in the past three years, companies attracting investor interest are largely opting for names that are both distinctive and vague.
  • Industry observers note that examples of this stylistic direction abound among the most heavily funded newer startups.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Startup naming tends to be a cyclical endeavor. For a few years, founders might be enamoured of silly monikers, made-up words, and creative misspellings. Then the pendulum swings, and startups defer to simple names that describe what they actually do.

So where are we now? Probably somewhere in the middle.

Per a Crunchbase analysis of startups 1 founded in the past three years, companies attracting investor interest are largely opting for names that are both distinctive and vague. It’s a preference that reflects this era of fast-evolving AI, in which founders want room to adapt.

Industry observers note that examples of this stylistic direction abound among the most heavily funded newer startups. There’s Also, which is of course a micromobility spin-out. Perplexity is a genAI organization although you couldn’t tell that by its name. And then there’s Sunday, which makes household robots, in case that wasn’t clear from the name.

“Reality is a lot of these companies, in seven or eight years they’ve done at least one or two major pivots,” Athol Foden, who runs the naming consultancy Brighter Naming, told us. That makes it logical to pick a name that can still work afterward.

When startups do make inventive picks, it’s often out of necessity rather than preference.

“We’re running out of words. Everything is trademarked multiple times over,” said Bruno Benedini, co-founder of branding consultancy Taillight. “So we have to look for something unexpected.

Given that reality, Benedini is always on the lookout for startups that exemplify the element of surprise. One standout is Hugging Face, the AI model sharing and development platform, which Nvidia agreed to acquire for $12.9 billion in September. It didn’t succeed just because of its strange name, obviously, but it didn’t hurt.

Another more recent upstart that caught his attention is Flapping Airplanes, an AI research lab that raised a $1 billion Series A last month.

Industry observers note that “It’s super playful, but you remember it, and you have this visual,” he said. Plus, it’s not the kind of name one’s lawyer finds is already taken by a competitor.

According to recent reports, the AI boom is also often characterized as a period in which companies are building the foundational layer of a technology that will fundamentally transform our lives for decades to come. Given this mindset, it’s perhaps predictable that we’re seeing a plethora of names with themes tied to building and industry.

According to recent reports, foden points to Databricks as one of the more longstanding representatives of this naming approach. Its brand evokes the notion of digital data as one small component of a massive building endeavor.

According to recent reports, but newer upstarts are onto this trend as well. There’s an abundance of recently founded companies with “foundation” in their name, for instance, including Foundation Health, Foundation Industries, Foundational Industries, Foundational and Foundation.

Another recent example with an industrial, maker vibe is Blacksmith, a cloud infrastructure startup founded in 2024 that’s pulled in more than $100 million this year.

Industry observers note that dating app Rivet looks like a more unusual sector match for an industrial name. The two-year-old startup runs a platform in which volunteer matchmakers pick matches for daters.

Nuclear startup Standard Nuclear, meanwhile, reads like a twist on Gilded Age industrial giant Standard Oil.

There’s also a continuing effort to add a humanizing element to AI and robotics technologies. After all, no one wants to patronize a company called “AI-Enabled Robotics Overlord Who Will Soon Be Taking Your Job.”.

It’s not just newer startups applying this tactic. Startups have a long history of going with popular first names as brands. And of course Anthropic has secured massive market share  of late with a chatbot and coder named Claude.

Newer funded startups with first name-based brands include Theo, Henry, Clara and Mira, among others. Then there’s Humans&, an AI startup that’s taking a different route to attempt a humanizing brand.

Of course, nowadays it’s not even necessary to confer with a human when generating naming ideas. You can just ask AI for suggestions.

Per Benedini, the technology’s not there yet.

Sources indicate that “We still use AI to see what it comes up with, and it’s like 99% garbage,” he remarked. Moreover, selecting a name is only the first step — one must also determine if it’s available for use.

Still, it’s early days. Perhaps in the future it will be AI naming AI companies to appeal to other AI agents. But hopefully there will still be a role for us to play going forward.

Sample set was limited to startups in English-speaking countries. ↩.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Wednesday's inflows narrowed the net outflow gap for XRP ETFs.
  • That means the net outflows over the rest of the period totaled $25.32 million.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that U.S. spot exchange-traded funds for XRP recorded net inflows of $4.07 million on Nov. 25. XRP was the only cryptocurrency among the 10 ETF categories tracked in a SoSoValue snapshot shared by BankXRP to register net inflows.

Wednesday's inflows narrowed the net outflow gap for XRP ETFs. Following the latest inflows, XRP funds had recorded $21.25 million more in investor outflows than inflows over the 30 days ending Nov. 25.

That means the net outflows over the rest of the period totaled $25.32 million. In a single trading day, investors covered about 16% of that shortfall.

The five U.S. spot XRP ETFs tracked by SoSoValue at the moment have total net assets of $1.04 billion. This is marginally higher than the $1 billion held by nine spot Solana ETFs.

However, there is a larger disparity in cumulative net inflows between XRP and Solana funds. Cumulative net inflows total $1.79 billion for XRP and $1.51 billion for Solana.

Recent findings suggest that the two figures measure different things. Cumulative net inflows represent the total amount of money invested in the funds minus redemptions.

Net assets, on the other hand, represent the current value of a fund's holdings. This figure changes with the price of XRP.

This explains why XRP funds have a little over $1 billion in net assets despite attracting nearly $1.8 billion in cumulative net inflows.

Trading activity was slightly higher in Solana ETFs on Wednesday, with total volume reaching $35.54 million, compared to $33.40 million for XRP.

However, Solana ETFs recorded zero net flows for the day.

Investors can trade existing ETF shares with one another without affecting the total amount of money invested in the funds.

The contrast with Bitcoin ETFs was stark.

It has been revealed that U.S. spot Bitcoin ETFs recorded $123.41 million in net outflows on Wednesday, according to preliminary figures reported by SoSoValue.

It has been revealed that however, the total for Bitcoin was still being compiled when BankXRP shared the numbers. SoSoValue marked the XRP total as complete.

With U.S. markets closed for Thanksgiving, XRP ETF buyers have only one more trading day this week.

Trading resumes on U.S. equity markets on Friday, Nov. 27. However, the session will end early, with markets closing at 1 p.m. Eastern time.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Nvidia’s equity in private companies continues to grow: It revealed its stakes are now worth $65.5 billion on Tuesday, up from the $22 billion reported in January. The increase includes both new investments and significant markups of existing portfolio companies.

According to recent reports, the company invested $16 billion into equities in the past quarter alone, it stated, and $58 billion in the past nine months of its fiscal year. This amount includes buying shares in public and private companies, yet it shows how the chipmaker made massive bets over the course of the year, especially compared to last year; in November 2025, the company reported spending $5 billion buying equity in the first nine months of that fiscal year.

But it’s unclear if this growth will continue under the interim CEO and Jensen Huang’s successor.

Nvidia stated in late 2023 that the goal of its corporate investing is to expand the AI ecosystem by backing startups it considers to be “game changers and market makers.”  Over the nearly three years that followed, the chipmaker has invested in nearly 350 startups, according to PitchBook. The companies Nvidia backed include Anthropic and OpenAI; neolabs like Thinking Machines and Reflection; neoclouds, like Lambda, Nscale, and Crusoe; as well as other companies developing AI infrastructure, robotics startups, and applications.

It’s also become a major financier of the data center build-out, reporting $118 billion in guarantees with $105 billion of that the backstop it supplied for OpenAI’s $500 billion data center in Ohio.

According to recent reports, the organization made those commitments by allocating a meaningful portion of its excess cash flows. In Tuesday’s earnings call, Kress noted Nvidia would continue providing financing assistance to strong customers and that “as the market matures and additional sources of capital become available,” the company would be “rigorously evaluating future investments, commitments, and guarantees.”.

But the question for the VC ecosystem is whether the manufacturer will continue to back startups at anywhere near the same level without Huang at the helm.

It has been revealed that huang’s rampant dealmaking has reportedly been a source of concern for Kress. Investors have told TechCrunch that they anticipate she will take a more conservative approach to startup investing, becoming more selective with new investments and writing smaller-sized checks into its existing portfolio companies.

Recent findings suggest that “We intend to return all excess free cash flow net of strategic uses to shareholders during this last quarter and going forward,” Kress said on the earnings call on Tuesday. Just how strategic startups will be under her leadership, and under the future permanent CEO, remains to be seen. But for now, VCs are bracing for a meaningful pullback in capital.

#169048. How Bittensor's Gamma Turns Every AI Payment Into an Alpha Burn

How Bittensor's Gamma Turns Every AI Payment Into an Alpha Burn

📅 11 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1726 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Nulltx

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Paying a Bittensor subnet with gamma burns its alpha token.
  • It has been revealed that using a subnet's service today usually means creating an account, adding funds and collecting an API key, and every additional subnet repeats the routine.
  • They can pay with TAO, and the protocol buys the subnet’s alpha and burns it in a single transaction.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

AI-assisted summary, reviewed by NullTX editors.

Paying a Bittensor subnet with gamma burns its alpha token. Here is how gamma gets minted, how the lower-price rule works and why the credit can never be converted back.Pay a Bittensor subnet for an AI answer with gamma, and your payment vanishes. The alpha token behind it gets burned, the credit gets spent, and nobody can redeem either one.

It has been revealed that using a subnet's service today usually means creating an account, adding funds and collecting an API key, and every additional subnet repeats the routine. Opentensor announced gamma to cut that friction. With gamma, a Bittensor wallet handles both access and payment across any subnet that adopts the standard.The mechanics are laid out in the gamma guide in the subtensor docs. Gamma is a credit a subnet can accept as payment, valued in US dollars. A customer gets it by burning that subnet's alpha token, and each dollar of burned alpha value mints one gamma, so a burn valued at $100 creates 100 gamma.Each balance stays tied to the subnet where it was created. Gamma minted for subnet 51 can't pay for a service on any other subnet. Root switches the system on network-wide, and each subnet owner or lease beneficiary then enables it for their own subnet.

Customers have two ways in. They can pay with TAO, and the protocol buys the subnet’s alpha and burns it in a single transaction. Or they can pay with alpha they already hold on that subnet, and the protocol burns it directly to create gamma.

Setup takes four steps. The customer creates a fresh hotkey that will act as an API key, associates it with their coldkey, looks up the service they want and mints. The docs give the command: btcli gamma mint --netuid 51 --hotkey API_KEY --amount-tao 10 --service-hotkey SERVICE_HOTKEY. The TAO route follows the same pool and flow accounting as stake-burn and creates no stake position. Owners who hold stake can burn it with mint-gamma-with-stake, and --amount-alpha all burns the whole position.

Recent findings suggest that the gamma lands in a deposit. Each deposit belongs to the minting coldkey and is keyed by the API-key hotkey, which signs the customer's requests. A hotkey holds at most one deposit per subnet, and a coldkey holds at most 64 per subnet. The docs warn against reusing a staking hotkey or a coldkey, because requests signed with the key get paid from the deposit.A few guardrails apply. A mint must reach at least 0.1 gamma. By default, the SDK quotes the mint first and fails it if the result lands more than 5% below the quote. The mint also needs a TAO/USD price no older than 300 blocks, about an hour.

It has been revealed that gamma’s valuation rule decides how much credit a burn buys. The protocol values the burned alpha in TAO, then converts that figure to dollars through an on-chain TAO/USD price feed. The TAO value equals alpha multiplied by the lower of two prices, the gamma price and the spot price, which the docs write as alpha × min(gamma price, spot price).

Every subnet keeps a gamma price. When a subnet registers, the price starts at the median alpha price across subnets. After that it moves asymmetrically. If spot falls, the gamma price falls to match at once. If spot rises, the gamma price climbs slowly toward it, closing a small slice of the gap each block, so the gap halves every 600 blocks, roughly two hours. However high spot jumps, the gamma price can at most double every 600 blocks.An example indicates the effect. Say a user burns 100 alpha when spot sits at 0.05 TAO but the gamma price lags at 0.04. The mint uses 0.04, which gives 4 TAO of value, and at $400 per TAO that mints 1,600 gamma. Had the gamma price caught up, the same burn would mint 2,000, so the lag costs the burner 400 gamma. A short-lived pump buys no extra credit. The figures are illustrative, but the rule comes straight from the docs.The TAO/USD feed gets similar damping. A root-controlled oracle supplies the price, and the accepted price falls to a lower feed immediately but rises at most 66 parts per million per block, about 2% an hour. The docs admit the oracle is trusted: its accepted price can climb up to roughly 61% a day until root replaces or removes it.One more detail matters. The docs say alpha is valued at these prices, not at what selling it would return, so a burn that is large relative to the pool is worth more than a sale would be. A substantial burner gets credit for full value instead of a slipped sale price.Once minted, gamma holds its dollar value whether TAO or alpha prices rise or fall. Service providers still set their own prices.

To use a service, a person or an AI agent signs a request with a hotkey from their Bittensor wallet. The subnet owner, or another authorized account, deducts the required credits from that hotkey's gamma balance before delivering the service. Nothing transfers to anyone. The designated spender calls `spend-gamma` with up to 512 entries per call, each naming a hotkey, an amount and a 32-byte reference, and the spent gamma is destroyed on the spot.The reference doubles as a receipt. By convention it holds the service's own ID for the request being paid, returned with the response, so the customer can match each spend to a specific request. The chain repeats the reference in its events and reads it nowhere else, so an entry sent twice spends twice.Customers keep control throughout. The minting coldkey can set a daily spend cap that refills linearly over 7,200 blocks, about a day, and a cap of zero pauses the deposit. The coldkey can also change the spender, keep separate deposits for different apps and agents, and top up an existing deposit without switching hotkeys. Because the coldkey can pause or redirect at any moment, services spend ahead: they spend what they are about to serve, then serve what was spent. A spender can hand this right to a `GammaSpend` proxy, which can make no other call.Both minting and spending leave public records on-chain, so anyone can audit how much credit a subnet has created and how much customers have used.

In a recent development, the limits are strict. Gamma can't be transferred to another wallet, and it can't be converted back into alpha or TAO. It confers no claim on any party and can't be redeemed. Each subnet chooses whether, and at what prices, it accepts its own gamma.

The docs flag the sharpest risk directly: dissolving or pruning a subnet destroys all of its gamma, and holders receive nothing. A customer who prepaid a large deposit to a subnet that later shuts down loses it. Moving gamma between your own deposits is allowed, and a deposit opened under someone else's hotkey stays yours, since you can pull the gamma back at any time.A coldkey swap adds a few wrinkles. While one is confirmed, the coldkey's gamma calls are refused, though its spenders keep spending. After a subnet owner swaps coldkeys, deposits that name the old one keep it until the owner republishes its service.

The docs answer the economic question in one sentence: spent gamma pays its spender nothing. The value of the burned alpha accrues to the subnet's alpha holders.

Sources indicate that that makes gamma a direct demand mechanism for alpha. Creating gamma always burns the subnet's alpha, which removes those tokens from circulation for good. When customers pay with TAO, the protocol first buys alpha from the subnet's pool, so TAO-funded purchases add buying pressure before the burn. Every dollar of AI usage ties a purchase of service credits to a burn of alpha.

In a recent development, A service operator earns through the alpha it holds and the emissions its subnet receives, not through a payment from customers. The structure rewards subnets that attract real usage, since usage shrinks their alpha supply.Two questions remain open. Customers get dollar-denominated credit, but the burn that funds it follows alpha prices, so heavy usage during a price spike may feel expensive. Holders also carry the dissolution risk, which will push careful buyers toward established subnets. Which services accept gamma, and at what price, will show whether this becomes a real payments layer or a niche tool. The mechanism is clear, and adoption is the unknown.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Album VC, a Lehi, Utah-based early-stage venture firm that’s been known until now as Peak Ventures, just gathered up $75 million in capital commitments for its third early-stage fund.

The development highlights investor confidence in Album’s young team, which came together in 2014 after the founder of Zinch — a site connecting colleges and students that sold to the ed-tech organization Chegg in 2011 — decided to try his hand at investing in other startups.

As that founder, Sid Krommenhoek — who stayed on with Chegg for several years, running its international efforts — explains it, “I thought I’d do another startup. But I also knew from our own experience in struggling to raise money the need for more capital in Utah, and I thought having that operator-entrepreneur perspective could be useful.”.

A first fund, like many in the industry, was more of an experiment, though it was a decent $23 million, thanks largely to the support of Chegg CEO Dan Rosensweig, who was early to commit capital to the fund. A second ($56 million) fund followed when Krommenhoek and John Mayfield — a friend who joined him from a marketing role at Qualtrics — began investing more seriously in their backyard and beyond.

They were soon joined by a third investor, Diogo Myrrha, who began as a principal with the firm and is now a general partner. Explains Krommenhoek of one of the many things that binds the three Brigham Young University grads, “We all came into Utah’s orbit when it wasn’t necessarily a place where you could live out your career, but that’s changed.”.

According to recent reports, the P vs NP question in computer science pops up in our feeds way more often than it did just a few days ago. No wonder—it's a problem mostly relevant and interesting to mathematicians and computer scientists, and it's also a Clay Millennium Prize problem. It asks a relatively simple question: whether every problem whose solution can be checked quickly can also be solved quickly.

Short answer: no, it can't. P vs NP is an efficiency question. NP is about whether a proposed solution can be checked efficiently, while P covers problems that computers can solve efficiently. For example, solving a complicated Sudoku certainly takes time, but checking the result is not as hard.

In a recent development, the question itself simply asks whether every checkable problem has an efficient solution. P ≠ NP says that some problems are harder to solve than to verify, and that is a core question: most scientists expect P ≠ NP, but proving it is the hard part.

It has been revealed that cryptography is purely mathematical, so issues relevant to computation apply here. ZK-proofs represent a more relevant crypto technology used every day and connected to NP: a statement (such as a transaction) is proven without revealing additional data (a zero-knowledge proof).

But the question is different: could it raise any problems, cause security concerns, or lead to exploits? To some extent—yes. Public-key cryptography is certainly something that can be affected right away—as can blockchains, wallets, and even HTTPS—but P=NP alone wouldn't break the whole industry.

Recent findings suggest that not really, because you can't change the fundamental math. Even if consensus mechanisms are changed and networks are upgraded, it would be similar to solving 2=2. It's fundamental. But instead of 'solving' it, cryptocurrency projects might adapt to such challenges. New systems might avoid relying on assumptions, so such a change would be a reaction to the consequences.

Quantum computing is a different story. Unlike P vs NP, quantum computing is not just a theoretical question about computational complexity. It's a technological development that could directly affect existing cryptographic systems.

India’s Humyn Labs raises $47M to feed US robotics companies the data they need

💡 Key Takeaways
  • As demand grows for real-world data to train robots, India’s Humyn Labs has raised $47 million in Series A financing to help U.S.
  • According to recent reports, the funding comprises $26 million in equity led by Accel, with participation from Prosus Ventures, BeeGlobal, Bajaj Finance’s Finserv Intelligence and Bajaj Alts AI Opportunities Fund, Dallas Venture Capital, Lighthouse Canton, and Jump Trading.
  • According to recent reports, companies around the world are trying to build robots capable of performing everyday human tasks, but getting enough quality data to train them remains difficult.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

As demand grows for real-world data to train robots, India’s Humyn Labs has raised $47 million in Series A financing to help U.S. AI and robotics companies build models that can operate in physical environments.

According to recent reports, the funding comprises $26 million in equity led by Accel, with participation from Prosus Ventures, BeeGlobal, Bajaj Finance’s Finserv Intelligence and Bajaj Alts AI Opportunities Fund, Dallas Venture Capital, Lighthouse Canton, and Jump Trading. It also includes $21 million in venture debt led by Lighthouse Canton, with participation from Trifecta Capital.

According to recent reports, companies around the world are trying to build robots capable of performing everyday human tasks, but getting enough quality data to train them remains difficult. Startups, including Mecka AI, XDOF, and MicroAGI, are already tackling the problem by collecting real-world data for robotics training. Bengaluru-based Humyn Labs aims to compete with them.

Industry observers note that humyn Labs has developed its own two-camera hardware to record people performing everyday tasks. It then uses its software to process and label the footage, which means tagging what happens in each clip so AI can learn from it. The startup collects data across over 20 countries in Latin America and Asia, with Brazil, India, and South Korea serving as its main hubs, co-founder Manish Agarwal (pictured above, right) stated in an interview.

Agarwal, the former CEO of Indian gaming company Nazara Technologies, founded Humyn Labs in February with Ishank Gupta (pictured above, left), a former executive at the brewing giant AB InBev. The duo previously founded Kratos Studios, now known as KGeN. KGeN has a network of contributors across emerging markets, and that network helps Humyn Labs collect data in people’s homes, the founders told TechCrunch.

According to recent reports, collecting footage of human activity is only part of the challenge, Agarwal mentioned. He added that Humyn Labs also uses software to track hand movements, interactions with objects, and other details, turning raw recordings into data that AI models can learn from.

“Scale, diversity, and quality are important aspects, and they need to work in tandem,” Agarwal remarked.

It has been revealed that humyn Labs claims it has 12 paying customers, including frontier AI labs, robotics companies, and developers of world models. About 90% of its revenue comes from the U.S., Gupta said, though he declined to name specific customers.

The startup generated $10 million in revenue between April and October and has another $20 million in signed contracts, Agarwal told TechCrunch, adding that a further $20 million in deals has yet to be finalized.

Industry observers note that that growth has also increased Humyn Labs’ need for working capital, Agarwal said, explaining the $21 million venture debt component. The startup pays workers and data collection partners daily or weekly but typically waits 30 to 60 days to receive payments from its AI lab customers. Borrowing helps bridge that gap and is less dilutive than selling more equity, he said.

It has been revealed that over the last few months, India has emerged as a hub for collecting training data for so-called physical AI, with startups, including Human Archive and BuildAI, tapping into the country’s large workforce to record people performing everyday tasks. However, the practice has also raised questions about privacy and consent, particularly when people are recorded inside their homes.

Agarwal said Humyn Labs collects data from people doing their usual work or household chores instead of asking them to perform staged activities. The startup works with local partners to identify collection sites and oversee the process. “The worker is a worker who is incentivized, but he needs to be monitored and supervised for the right input,” he stated.

Humyn Labs currently has 51 full-time employees, most based in Bengaluru, plus a network of local partners across the countries where it collects data, Agarwal stated.

Industry observers note that A Zcash (ZEC) whale that bought 23,412 ZEC nine years ago moved 15,750 ZEC worth $11.39 million after nine years of inactivity, Lookonchain reported on Thursday. According to Lookonchain, the whale paid $5.04 million for the coins at an average price of $215.

Lookonchain also said that after nine years of holding, the whale was finally selling, and that his total profit on the position was more than $12 million.

It has been revealed that arkham data demonstrates that the whale sent the ZEC in two transactions. The first one, 8,000 ZEC worth $5.73 million, went to an address without an Arkham label. About an hour later, the wallet sent 7,750 ZEC worth $5.66 million to a Kraken deposit address.

The whale got the coins nine years ago from Zcash's shielded pool. He withdrew most of them in batches of 250 ZEC, according to Arkham.

On Thursday, Lookonchain also reported that another whale deposited about 47,500 ZEC, or $35.8 million, to Binance.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that as businesses increasingly turn to AI agents to automate work, the vast amounts of information locked in complex documents remain a challenge.
  • In a recent development, silicon Valley venture capital firm Felicis led the round, with participation from Y Combinator, Orange Collective, and Uncorrelated Ventures.
  • Business documents often include tables, charts, and complicated layouts that AI systems can struggle to interpret accurately.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that as businesses increasingly turn to AI agents to automate work, the vast amounts of information locked in complex documents remain a challenge. Unsiloed AI has raised $7.5 million in seed funding led by Felicis to tackle that problem, aiming to help enterprises make their documents more accessible to AI agents through specialized technology.

In a recent development, silicon Valley venture capital firm Felicis led the round, with participation from Y Combinator, Orange Collective, and Uncorrelated Ventures. Angel investors Aarthi Ramamurthy and Beth Turner also participated.

Business documents often include tables, charts, and complicated layouts that AI systems can struggle to interpret accurately. But getting the information wrong can lead to costly mistakes for businesses, and the impact could be severe in the case of a bank, hospital, or a law firm, as they rely on these documents for their daily work.

According to recent reports, unsiloed aims to solve this problem with software that breaks down complex documents, extracts information from tables, charts, and other elements, and turns it into structured data that AI agents can use. The technology also reveals where the extracted information came from in the original document, so businesses can check the results rather than take the AI’s output at face value.

“The problem with LLMs is they’re inherently probabilistic,” remarked Unsiloed co-founder and CEO Aman Mishra (pictured above, right) in an interview. “There is going to be some deviation induced. There is going to be some hallucination involved, and that has a massive negative impact downstream.”.

Mishra co-founded Unsiloed with Adnan Abbas (pictured above, left), his former classmate at the Indian Institute of Technology (IIT) Kharagpur. The two joined Y Combinator’s Fall 2025 batch after spending some time developing the technology.

Recent findings suggest that unsiloed is already working with customers in finance, legal services, and healthcare, Mishra told TechCrunch. One bank is using its technology to process documents, while a law firm has deployed it on its own servers to handle contracts and old case files, he said, without naming either customer. Mishra, however, named voice AI startup Bolna AI as a customer, saying it uses Unsiloed to ingest knowledge bases for building voice agents.

The San Francisco-headquartered startup has entered a market that is already crowded and includes specialized document-processing startups such as Reducto and Unstructured, as well as offerings from Microsoft and Amazon. Businesses also sometimes use general-purpose AI models to extract information from documents, giving Unsiloed another set of competitors.

In a recent development, mishra told TechCrunch that Unsiloed’s advantage lies in how it processes complex documents. The startup uses what it calls “dual-stream” vision models, which handle text and image data separately, along with a technique called “heat map-based chunking” that helps identify the most notable parts of a document.

Sources indicate that “In one of the streams you have the text tokens, in the other stream you have the exact image tokens,” Mishra remarked. “This is something that we have spent a lot of time architecting.”.

The technology then directs more computing power toward areas such as figures, numbers, and charts. Unsiloed also uses a specialized decoder that takes industry-specific terminology into account, helping it distinguish between terms that can mean different things in different business contexts.

Supporting those claims, Mishra pointed to a test involving 542 financial documents supplied by an enterprise customer. Unsiloed achieved 99.78% accuracy across roughly 84,000 extracted data points, per a technical brief shared by the startup. The test compared Unsiloed with major AI models, Microsoft’s Azure Document Intelligence, and the customer’s in-house extraction tool. The results have, however, not been independently verified.

Unsiloed also claims to have outperformed competing AI document-processing tools on olmOCR-Bench, a public benchmark developed by Allen AI. In tests conducted by the startup, Unsiloed scored 88.0, compared with 66.0 for Reducto’s agentic system and 39.9 for Unstructured. The benchmark covered 1,403 PDF pages and tested how well the systems handled tables, mathematical expressions, scanned documents, and complex layouts.

Unsiloed’s pricing, Mishra said, starts at one cent per page. He asserted that the startup’s approach also helps keep its costs down by directing computing power toward the parts of a document that need the most attention, instead of processing every section in the same way.

Recent findings suggest that currently, Unsiloed has a headcount of seven people. The startup, Mishra noted, plans to use the fresh funding to hire more researchers and engineers, expand its sales efforts, and develop proprietary datasets to improve its technology.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that in today’s world, all professional employees use AI, whether it’s candidates submitting highly polished CVs with 100% perfect fit with your job description to AI-generated work. In this environment, how can we promote the right employees and how do we hire the best canidates when everyone appears to be perfect?

Imagine this: You’re hiring a financial analyst and give two finalists the same AI-generated acquisition memo. It reads beautifully and recommends buying a company at what looks like a reasonable price. There’s one problem. The model counted the same revenue twice.

One candidate improves the slides. The other asks for the source data, spots the error and changes the recommendation. If I’d asked for a polished take-home assignment and used AI to grade it, I might have hired the better slide editor.

Industry observers note that AI has become a significant part of how people apply for jobs and how they do that work. Using AI to police that behavior is a losing game. Employers have more to gain by making AI use visible and designing hiring and performance reviews around what people do with it.

Indeed illustrates both sides of the hiring loop. Its Career Scout offers job seekers résumé help, while its employer tools help review applications against hiring criteria. Both can save time, and résumé assistance can help a qualified applicant explain experience they’ve struggled to put into words.

But it can also make two very different candidates look equally well-suited for a role on paper.

An AI detector adds another score without answering the question the employer cares about: Could this person do the job?

I’d use AI to help the recruiter prepare a better follow-up. If someone says they led an integration, ask them to walk through a decision they made when two teams disagreed. The résumé gets you to the question. The answer gives you something to evaluate.

CoderPad offers an interview environment where candidates use AI on realistic tasks while interviewers watch how they prompt, evaluate and revise the output. That gives employers a practical way to observe a skill candidates will increasingly need on the job.

In a recent development, I’d give every finalist the same flawed acquisition memo, the same source documents and access to the same AI tools. Then I’d ask what they would verify before sending the memo to a client. One might catch the double-counted revenue. Another might go further and work out whether the corrected numbers change the price we should offer. The most revealing moment may come when the tool confidently insists its original calculation was right. What does the candidate do then?

Lattice lets managers use AI to draft reviews from goals, feedback and meeting notes. Synq, formerly Gloat, states its software can build and run a review cycle from a plain-English instruction. These tools make it easier to collect and summarize evidence. That makes the choice of what to collect more consequential.

Breaking: Enjin Matrixchain Votes on OpenGov Today: What Changes for ENJ Holders on November 16

📅 13 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1549 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Nulltx

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that enjin holders vote through November 13 on moving Matrixchain to OpenGov on November 16.
  • In a recent development, enjin's new proposal deposit sounds steep at 1,000 ENJ.
  • Recent findings suggest that enjin holders have until today, November 13, to vote on moving the Matrixchain to the Fort Canning release.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

AI-assisted summary, reviewed by NullTX editors.

Industry observers note that enjin holders vote through November 13 on moving Matrixchain to OpenGov on November 16. Here is how the nine tracks, the 1,000 ENJ deposit and conviction voting work, and what the Relaychain vote shows.

In a recent development, enjin's new proposal deposit sounds steep at 1,000 ENJ. It's actually the cheap part.

Recent findings suggest that enjin holders have until today, November 13, to vote on moving the Matrixchain to the Fort Canning release. The referendum opened November 10. If it passes, the upgrade is targeted for November 16 at block #12,319,600, with the network moving from runtime 1.3.1 to 1.4.3. Enjin's Fort Canning announcement lays out the plan, and the official changelog carries the technical detail.

In a recent development, the Relaychain has already made the jump. Referendum #16 approved its upgrade on October 28, and it went live on November 9. The Matrixchain vote is the second half of one upgrade, and it is the half that changes how Matrixchain makes decisions from then on.

Early coverage reported the schedule and the headline numbers: nine tracks, 1,000 ENJ. The changelog and the governance portal show the mechanics behind them, and those mechanics change more than the headlines suggest.

Today, the Matrixchain runs its governance through the older Democracy, Council and Technical Committee pallets, the modules that handle proposals and votes. Fort Canning replaces all three with a newly introduced set: Referenda, Conviction Voting, Origins, Whitelist and the Enjin Fellowship. Under OpenGov, any account can submit a referendum on one of nine tracks, and from the moment the upgrade lands, Matrixchain's own upgrades go through that process.

A track is a lane for a particular kind of decision. Enjin's changelog describes the families: Root and the admin tracks for the highest-stakes changes, Whitelisted Caller for proposals the Fellowship fast-tracks, and two special tracks, Referendum Killer and Referendum Canceller, for stopping a proposal that shouldn't proceed. Matrixchain gets no treasury tracks: those, sized by how much a proposal would spend, stay on the Relaychain, where treasury requests now go. Each track has its own deposit, approval curve and enactment period, and the Enjin Fellowship can fast-track time-sensitive proposals.

Splitting decisions this way means a small treasury request doesn't face the same bar as a change to the chain's core. Riskier tracks demand larger deposits and more support, while smaller ones move faster and cost less.

The submission deposit rises from 0.025 ENJ to 1,000 ENJ on every track, a 40,000-fold increase. The deposit is refunded when a referendum passes or is canceled, and it exists to deter spam. As an illustration, using the roughly $66 million market cap reported in early October, ENJ traded near three cents, which would put 1,000 ENJ around $33.

That is only the entry ticket. The cost that matters comes next. A referendum also needs a decision deposit before it moves into voting, and the changelog lists steep figures: 2,500,000 ENJ on Root and Fellowship Admin, 1,000,000 ENJ on the other admin tracks, and 2,500 to 250,000 ENJ on the Relaychain's treasury tracks. At the same illustrative price, the 2.5 million ENJ Root deposit comes to roughly $80,000, about 0.12% of the 2.02 billion ENJ total issuance.

So proposing is cheap, and pushing a proposal through is not. Anyone can raise an idea, but anyone who wants the network to vote on something substantial needs real stake in the outcome. The changelog says the same values apply on both chains, and Matrixchain adopts them for its newly introduced tracks.

It has been revealed that the best evidence of how these votes work comes from the Relaychain referendum that has already finished. Enjin's governance portal highlights referendum #16 as finalised, approved on October 28 and enacted on November 9.

Sources indicate that the final tally on the page is small. Eleven voters cast 381,303.02 ENJ of conviction-weighted voting power, and all of it went to Aye: 100% in favor, 0 ENJ against. The page also indicates raw, unweighted support of 271,303.2 ENJ, which it describes as the total balance backing the proposal and the figure the support curve uses. The conviction multiplier on the page runs from under 1x up to 6x.

Industry observers note that two numbers stand out. First, an entire chain upgrade passed with 271,303 ENJ of raw support, about 0.013% of the 2.02 billion ENJ total issuance, a figure worked out from the portal's number. Second, conviction added about 110,000 ENJ of weight on top of the raw balance, an average multiplier of roughly 1.4x. Voters picked up some extra weight, but most didn't lock their tokens for the long periods that earn the top multipliers.

A 100% Aye result says little by itself. A scheduled upgrade with no organized opposition passes easily, and the tally shows how thin engagement was.

In a recent development, fort Canning adds the safeguard that thin turnout calls for. A referendum now needs a minimum share of total ENJ voting in support. The changelog sets 0.5% on Root and the admin tracks, 0.005% to 0.125% on the Relaychain's treasury tracks, 0.1% for Referendum Killer and 0.05% for Referendum Canceller. Measured against 2.02 billion ENJ, that means about 10.1 million ENJ on Root, roughly 101,000 to 2.5 million on the treasury tracks, about 2.02 million to kill a referendum and about 1.01 million to cancel one.

It has been revealed that referendum #16's 271,303 ENJ of raw support would clear the lowest treasury floor of about 101,000 ENJ, but it would miss the Root floor by a factor of about 37. The page doesn't show which track the referendum used, and a runtime upgrade typically sits on a high-stakes track, so the Root comparison works as an illustration and not as a finding. The floors also didn't exist when #16 passed, since Fort Canning introduced them.

Sources indicate that that is the real change. Under the fresh rules, 11 wallets can't carry a chain-level decision on their own. Low turnout means failure, and proposals that matter will need far more ENJ behind them. Enjin's changelog claims Matrixchain upgrades go through OpenGov starting with this one, which suggests today's vote still runs on the current system, so the floors will first bite on the first OpenGov referendum.

Holders who haven't voted can still do so through Enjin's governance portal before the window closes. Voting locks tokens, so the lock length is worth checking first. Enjin's support article on voting explains the trade-off: the longer the lock, the more a vote counts, and tokens stay locked until the period ends.

According to recent reports, node operators on the Matrixchain can wait for the result before upgrading, as Enjin has indicated, and then follow the changelog for the version to install. Relaychain operators already needed client version 1.8.1.

According to recent reports, this vote is more about control than speed. OpenGov spreads decisions across tracks with deposits and support floors built for the weight of each choice, and it moves ENJ holders from voting on a handful of items to a standing governance system. The Relaychain's first vote revealed how little participation it took under the old rules, and the first referenda after November 16 will show whether holders turn out for the newly introduced ones. If most proposals stall at the decision deposit, the system costs too much. If they clear with a handful of voters, the floors aren't doing their job. Either result will tell holders what their ENJ can do.

Tech Report: New Bitcoin Core Upgrade: Breaking Down the Details

📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (444 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: U

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The key reason behind the setup is error handling in a way where there's no break in wallet usage that needs manual intervention in the process, to a significant degree.
  • Recent findings suggest that the pull request follows two earlier fixes, one for unnamed legacy wallets and another for crashes when Bitcoin Core couldn't write to the wallet directory, on the whole.
  • This isn't the first fix for wallet migration either, in the actual application.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The key reason behind the setup is error handling in a way where there's no break in wallet usage that needs manual intervention in the process, to a significant degree. Indeed, a Bitcoin wallet migration change was, broadly speaking, merged on November 25 by Bitcoin Core.

Recent findings suggest that the pull request follows two earlier fixes, one for unnamed legacy wallets and another for crashes when Bitcoin Core couldn't write to the wallet directory, on the whole. In fact, the thinking is to handle failures in a controlled way so the process can (to some degree) automatically restore the original wallet without needing manual intervention.

This isn't the first fix for wallet migration either, in the actual application.

Sources indicate that some mismatches during wallet creation could crash the graphical app or cause it to return a generic error. Those differences are now caught by Bitcoin Core and reported, which lets the migration process restore the original wallet from its backup, There are a couple of cases where the process could abruptly stop.

Industry observers note that trying to migrate a wallet in a read-only directory could also throw an error and skip cleanup, in real-world scenarios. In fact, now the process crashes with a clear error message. The test for this case is checking that the wallet is still in the old database format after the failure.

In a recent development, the biggest change is in how Bitcoin Core moves the wallet to SQLite. Earlier, it deleted the original database before writing the upcoming one. If something went wrong while making the new database or writing the wallet records, the user could end up restoring the backup by hand.

Industry observers note that now Bitcoin Core builds the SQLite database next to the original. So, the old database stays in place. These days, the latest one is being built. Once the wallet records have been written successfully, Bitcoin Core can move the new database into place. The pull request also tests this with a wallet stored on a separate filesystem.

A leftover SQLite journal in the wallet directory can corrupt the fresh database if SQLite uses it for the migrated wallet. In fact, Bitcoin Core now stops the migration when it finds a file, and the test checks that the journal stays in place. Moreover, the wallet keeps its legacy format.

It has been revealed that it's significant to keep in mind that automatic recovery still hinges on the backup being copied back successfully. As Ryan Ofsky mentioned in his review, if that copy crashes, the user still has to restore the backup by hand, on the whole.

But the Federal Reserve's preferred inflation gauge, the Personal Consumption Expenditures (PCE) price index, rose 3.8% year-over-year in October, up from 3.6% in September and matching a three-year high set in May. Core PCE, which excludes food and energy prices, rose 3.3%, compared with economists' expectations of 3.2% and September's reading of 3.1%.

Recent findings suggest that “America's inflation problem is bigger than an energy shock,” Heather Long, chief economist at Navy Federal Credit Union, told AFP. Consumer spending increased in dollar terms in October but was flat after adjusting for inflation.

In a recent development, A growing economy gives the Fed more room to raise borrowing costs to bring inflation back toward its 2% target. After Wednesday's inflation release, traders were pricing in a 98% probability of a quarter-point increase in December, according to CME FedWatch data. Today odds are set at 94%.

Industry observers note that the Fed held rates at between 3.75% and 4% in October after raising them in September for the first time in three years. Traders are also betting on further tightening in 2027, with another increase expected as early as January.

Recent findings suggest that the Office of the U.S. Trade Representative proposed tariffs targeting 14 economies, including China, the European Union, Japan and South Korea, following investigations into government policies that encourage manufacturing production beyond market demand.

The proposed rates vary by country and product, with duties of up to 20% on some Chinese imports and up to 35% on Vietnamese goods, subject to adjustments and exemptions. For the EU, the proposed 15% rate accounts for certain existing duties rather than simply adding 15 percentage points to them.

Recent findings suggest that the tariffs have not taken effect, and public hearings are scheduled to begin January 25. If importers pass the additional costs on to consumers, the duties could make the Fed's job of bringing inflation down even harder.

Meanwhile, Wall Street's enthusiasm over Jensen Huang's return to Nvidia didn't last very long. The chipmaker closed Monday up 31.5% but lost more than 6% Tuesday, while Anthropic closed at $81.91, below its $83 initial public offering price less than a week after its Nasdaq debut.

It has been revealed that higher interest rates make it more expensive to finance data centers and reduce the present value of future earnings. Both are particularly relevant for AI companies spending heavily today in anticipation of profits years down the road.

Sources indicate that the selloff began well before Wall Street opened. South Korea's Kospi closed 6.16% lower, while spot gold fell 2% to $3,483.59 an ounce by 9:15 a.m. ET, according to Reuters.

In a recent development, crypto investors were already in bad shape before Wednesday's economic data came out. Blockchain analytics firm Glassnode reported Tuesday that Bitcoin investors were realizing their heaviest losses since the collapse of FTX and the subsequent market crash in November 2022, relative to the money that flowed into the asset over the preceding year.

U.S. spot Bitcoin ETFs have also recorded $4.94 billion in net outflows this November through Tuesday, according to Decrypt’s ETF tracker, already making it their worst month since launching in January 2024.

The Fed's next interest rate decision is scheduled for December 9.
